items.title: Beyond Words: Making Space for Creative and Relational Approaches With Young Aboriginal Mothers in Central Australia.
items.authors: Reissenberger G, Abala S.
items.abstract: Young Aboriginal mothers in Central Australia experience both significant strengths and complex challenges in relation to social and emotional wellbeing, shaped through cultural identity, kinship, family responsibilities and broader social contexts. This commentary reflects on a small community pilot involving four creative and yarning-based sessions with two young Aboriginal mothers in Alice Springs. Guided by Yarning and Dadirri-informed deep listening, the programme created a culturally responsive, non-clinical space for artmaking, storytelling and shared reflection. Drawing on this experience, we reflect on making space for creative expression, relational connection and women's own understandings of wellbeing. We consider the opportunities and challenges of incorporating these approaches into maternal and family wellbeing initiatives, including the need for trust, flexible participation and culturally responsive facilitation. Meaningful integration requires attention to these conditions, alongside centring Aboriginal women's voices, cultural knowledge and relational understandings of wellbeing in health promotion practice.

items.title: Learning lattice parameters from powder X-ray diffraction data using invariants.
items.authors: Hofgard E, Min K, Segal N, Mittan-Moreau DW, Tehrani AM, Oklejas V, Gómez-Bombarelli R, Nigam J, Paley DW, Brewster AS, Smidt T.
items.abstract: We present a machine learning (ML) method to determine unit-cell parameters from powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) data using a novel invariant lattice representation. In ML, the data representation used can have a substantial impact on the prediction quality. Previous approaches have directly predicted lattice parameters (a, b, c, α, β, γ) from XRD inputs. However, these parameters depend strongly on the unit-cell reduction or convention used. In this work, we construct an invariant representation of the reciprocal lattice that is independent of primitive-cell convention, based on the bispectrum - a descriptor built from spherical harmonic projections of lattice points. The calculation of the lattice bispectrum is differentiable, and we demonstrate how to invert it using gradient-based optimization initialized from a nearest-neighbor lookup. We show that, with a fixed ML model architecture, using the lattice bispectrum as the ML target rather than the unit-cell parameters leads to more accurate lattice parameter predictions. For example, using the MP-20 dataset, a subset of the Materials Project database, the bispectrum reduces length mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 11.08% to 2.43% and angle MAPE from 12.15% to 2.45% compared with direct prediction with the same model architecture. We additionally benchmark our approach against pre-existing XRD data to crystal structure models such as Crystalyze and assess its performance on experimental data. Beyond unit-cell representation, we anticipate this invariant lattice representation could serve more broadly as a geometry-aware target for other crystallographic ML tasks such as structure generation.

items.title: Acceptability of Teledentistry in Mobile Oral Health Applications for Australian Children: A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: Groundwater J, Aiyar R, Jamieson L, Tiwari T, Kruger E, Tennant M, Nath S.
items.abstract:
Issues addressed

Access to timely dental care remains inequitable for children in rural, remote and disadvantaged communities. Teledentistry could narrow this gap, and mobile oral health apps offer a platform, yet user acceptance remains largely unexamined. This study explored how parents, public health professionals, software and design professionals and dental professionals perceive a teledentistry feature within a children's oral health app, and the equity and governance issues it raises.

Methods

Parents and caregivers, public health professionals, software and design professionals and dental professionals were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, social media and organisational contacts. Participants completed an online questionnaire capturing demographic characteristics and perceptions of mobile oral health technologies, followed by a semi-structured interview conducted in person, by telephone or via videoconference by one of four researchers. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Questionnaire data were summarised descriptively, and interviews were analysed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. Two researchers coded the data and developed preliminary themes.

Results

A total of 59 participants (39 women, 20 men) were interviewed, and four themes were developed: (1) acceptance of a teledentistry feature within a mobile oral health application; (2) the potential for teledentistry to improve access and equity; (3) preferences for in-person care, reflecting concerns about diagnostic accuracy, communication and clinician-patient relationships; and (4) perceived logistical and governance challenges to implementation. Participants viewed teledentistry as an acceptable, complementary feature for screening, triage, follow-up and continuity of care, recognising its potential to reduce geographical, social and systemic barriers, particularly for rural and isolated paediatric populations. However, concerns persisted that diagnostic accuracy, communication, trust and cultural safety are difficult to replicate remotely, alongside logistical and governance challenges including cost, funding, workforce capacity, oversight and safeguarding.

Conclusions

Teledentistry has the potential to improve equitable access to oral healthcare for children and families. However, its effectiveness depends on careful design and on its recognition as a trusted supplement to, rather than a replacement for, in-person care. This approach requires strong governance, sustainable funding and child-safe consent. SO WHAT?: Teledentistry is likely to be accepted by families and professionals only when it is positioned as an adjunct that extends, rather than substitutes for, in-person paediatric dental care. Developers and policymakers should therefore prioritise triage, follow-up and continuity functions, with clear pathways to a clinician and attention to cultural safety.

items.title: Mental Health Staff Capability and Practice for Promoting Physical Activity: Evidence From a Mental Health Community-Managed Organisation.
items.authors: Lamble R, Wirtu G, Watkins A, Orr M, Curtis J, Gagnon L, Ryall J, Fibbins H, Haywood D, Caperchione CM, Simmons D, Fletcher T, Hart NH, Rosenbaum S, Lederman O.
items.abstract:
Issue addressed

People with complex mental health conditions experience substantial reductions in life expectancy, largely due to preventable chronic disease. Mental health community-managed organisations (CMOs) are well placed to support physical health, yet little is known about staff capability to promote physical activity (PA).

Methods

A cross-sectional survey was administered to staff at a CMO in Sydney. Staff barriers, attitudes, confidence and knowledge relating to PA and physical health were assessed using the Physical Activity Attitudes Confidence Knowledge (PACK) and modified Metabolic Barriers Attitudes Confidence Knowledge (mM-BACK) questionnaires. PA promotional practices and personal PA behaviours were also assessed and relationships between these factors explored.

Results

Fifty-six of 78 eligible staff (72%) completed the survey. Mean scores were 34.8/45 (SD = 3.6) on PACK and 43.8/65 (SD = 6.7) on mM-BACK. Perceived barriers were generally low; workload was among those most commonly identified. Across both tools, attitudes scored highest, while confidence and knowledge scored lower. Only 23% reported familiarity with PA guidelines. Although 82% discussed PA with clients in the previous five workdays, 63% made no formal referrals. In correlation analyses, PA conversations were associated with mM-BACK attitudes (ρ = 0.43, p < 0.001) and PACK confidence (ρ = 0.34, p = 0.011), while capability was not associated with referrals.

Conclusions

CMO staff held positive attitudes towards PA promotion and commonly discussed PA with clients, but gaps remain in confidence, knowledge and referral practices. SO WHAT?: Building workforce capability, clarifying referral pathways and embedding organisational support for PA promotion within mental health CMOs may help reduce preventable health inequities in this population.

items.title: Unhealthy Digital Marketing Among Aboriginal People in Australia: Findings From the #DigitalMob Pilot Study.
items.authors: Browne J, Lister N, Backholer K, Hill K, Crocetti A, Walker T, Atkinson-Briggs S, Pathirana NL, Cubillo B, Martino F, Sherriff S, Yeomans L, Mitchell F, Thow S, Nguyen P, Ananthapavan J, Allender S, Paradies Y.
items.abstract:
Issue addressed

This study aimed to quantify Aboriginal adults' exposure to digital marketing of unhealthy food and beverages, alcohol, gambling, tobacco and e-cigarettes; analyse demographic differences in marketing exposure; and describe the nature of digital marketing reaching Aboriginal audiences, including brands, platforms and marketing tactics.

Methods

Thirty-one Aboriginal adults were asked to record their screens, capturing approximately one-third of their usual daily screen time (maximum 60 min). Recordings were analysed using SCANNER, an automated system trained to detect unhealthy commodity marketing. Demographic data and usual online behaviours were collected via an online survey. Descriptive statistics, a post hoc Mann-Whitney U test and a Fisher-Freeman-Halton extension of Fisher's Exact test were used to analyse differences in marketing detections.

Results

Most participants (n = 29/31, 94%) were exposed to unhealthy digital marketing. Of the 587 marketing instances detected, unhealthy food brands were most common (47%), followed by gambling (28%), alcohol (15%), sweetened beverages (9%) and tobacco (1%). No e-cigarette marketing was detected. Estimated daily exposure to unhealthy digital marketing was 40.4 (IQR: 11-92) instances per day. Male participants, aged 30 years and under, recorded significantly more marketing detections overall and for unhealthy food, alcohol and gambling brands.

Conclusion

Findings highlight the pervasiveness of unhealthy food and beverage, gambling and alcohol marketing in the everyday digital lives of Aboriginal participants. SO WHAT?: Comprehensive regulation of unhealthy digital marketing is urgently required to advance Aboriginal health.

items.title: The social origins of identity and bias: Language models, accumulated meaning and positioning.
items.authors: Durrheim K.
items.abstract: This paper develops a social psychological interpretation of distributional language models, algorithmically learned representations of natural language. Within these models, words are positioned according to patterns of usage, and the resulting embeddings can be interpreted as maps of cultural associations available for learning. This cultural-learning account explains how patterned meanings become available to individual cognition but leaves open how those meanings are socially produced. Drawing on social identity theory, discursive psychology and a stigmergic-dialogical model of communication, the paper argues that identity and bias emerge through social interaction and the accumulation of linguistic traces. As people take positions, respond to others and circulate formulations, they produce patterns of meaning that locate actors relationally and make alignments and differences recognizable. Bias emerges when this accumulation is uneven, making associations, evaluations and distinctions differentially available across communities. From this perspective, embeddings map patterns accumulated through social activity. Their geometry captures relations through which identities become recognizable and groups distinguishable. The paper extends this approach with speaker landscapes, which locate speakers by their language use and show how groups become differentiated. The result is a framework for studying how meaning, identity, bias and group differentiation are socially produced at scale.

items.title: Large Language Models in RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
items.authors: Verma PK, Ganesh S, Varadarajan S.
items.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative role of large language models (LLMs) in predicting RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs). By leveraging the sequence-based learning capabilities of LLMs, this chapter illustrates how these models can capture complex patterns in nucleotide sequences, structural motifs, and functional dependencies without explicit feature engineering. We discuss state-of-the-art architectures adapted for RNA data, including Transformer-based models and protein-inspired sequence embeddings, highlighting their performance in both supervised and self-supervised settings. Practical considerations for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs on RRI datasets are provided, alongside strategies to interpret model predictions using explainable AI approaches. Case studies demonstrate how LLMs can accelerate discovery in non-coding RNA regulation, RNA therapeutics design, and the broader transcriptomic landscape. Finally, challenges such as data sparsity, generalization to novel RNA families, and computational efficiency are examined, offering guidance for future research at the intersection of natural language processing and RNA biology.

items.title: Interventions to Enhance Organisational Health Literacy Responsiveness in Institutional and Community-Based Settings for Children: A Systematic Scoping Review.
items.authors: Wijeratne D, Amoah R, Kelly R, Elmer S, Nash R.
items.abstract:
Issue addressed

Organisational health literacy responsiveness (OHLR) reflects the capacity of healthcare, educational, and community organisations to respond and offer equitable access to health information and services. Evidence on interventions addressing children's health literacy needs across these settings remains fragmented. This review aimed to identify and characterise OHLR-related interventions and map their reported outcomes.

Methods

A scoping review was conducted following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Six electronic databases and grey literature sources were searched for literature published from 2005 to October 2025. Of 1494 records, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis and reported intervention outcomes were mapped against the seven-dimension Organisational Health Literacy Responsiveness (Org-HLR) framework.

Results

The 33 studies were conducted in 14 countries and across hospital, school, and community-based settings. Few interventions addressed all seven Org-HLR dimensions. Communication practices were addressed in all studies, followed by workforce development (n = 23) and access to services (n = 21). Fewer studies addressed system processes (n = 16), community engagement (n = 16), and leadership and culture (n = 15). Several interventions used participatory or co-design approaches. Reported outcomes included improved communication, workforce capacity, service accessibility, and user engagement. Long-term and system-level outcomes were rarely assessed.

Conclusions

To reduce inequity in service provision, services need to consider their OHLR. Interventions identified in this review show potential to strengthen organisational capacity to respond to carer and children's health literacy needs, but approaches remain heterogeneous, fragmented, and evidence on sustained organisational and system-level outcomes was limited. More research is warranted. SO WHAT?: OHLR could guide equitable health promotion across schools, child and family health services, and services supporting culturally and linguistically diverse communities. Cross-sector policies, workforce development, leadership, and meaningful participation can support the integration of OHLR into routine practice.

items.title: Annotating Tandem Mass Spectra in Metabolomics with DreaMS and MassSpecGym.
items.authors: Jozefov F, Bushuiev R, Bushuiev A, Hebra T, Damiani T, Šivic J, Pluskal T.
items.abstract: We present a simple, practical workflow for annotating tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data of small molecules using advanced machine learning and a reference library. The discovery and structural characterization of small molecules is central to biology, chemistry, and medicine. MS/MS has become the leading technology for this task, yet the majority of spectra from untargeted metabolomics remain unannotated, limiting our understanding of the underlying chemical diversity. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping many areas of science, and mass spectrometry is no exception. In this chapter, we introduce a practical workflow for annotating MS/MS data using two complementary resources: DreaMS, a foundation model for mass spectrometry, and MassSpecGym, a large reference library and benchmarking platform. DreaMS embeds mass spectra into a representation space where structural similarity is preserved, and MassSpecGym provides anchor points for retrieving identical or related molecules. Together, they form an ecosystem that enables efficient annotation of experimental MS/MS data. We demonstrate this approach on alkaloid data from Piper fimbriulatum, showing how DreaMS can retrieve exact matches or place unannotated spectra alongside structurally related compounds. All steps are provided as easy-to-follow protocols, designed to run on standard hardware and requiring no modifications to existing metabolomics pipelines. Readers will learn how to integrate AI tools into their own workflows for compound annotation, molecular networking, and discovery. Overall, this chapter aims to empower biologists and chemists to harness machine learning for metabolomics, transforming unannotated spectra into interpretable chemical knowledge.

items.title: Automated Quantification and Morphometric Analysis of Pluripotent Stem Cell Colonies Using ColonyQuant.
items.authors: Kidder BL.
items.abstract: Alkaline phosphatase staining is routinely used to evaluate the undifferentiated state of embryonic stem cells, yet quantitative interpretation of colony assays frequently depends on manual inspection and categorical scoring that introduce subjectivity and limit scalability. ColonyQuant provides a standardized, automated framework for objective analysis of alkaline phosphatase-stained colonies from conventional bright-field images. The software performs adaptive colony detection, per-colony intensity measurement, and extraction of eight geometric descriptors that collectively characterize colony size, compactness, symmetry, and boundary complexity. Feature tables generated by the workflow are structured to support statistical comparison across replicates and experimental conditions. Integrated analysis modules enable dimensionality reduction, supervised classification, and feature ranking, facilitating interpretation of phenotypic differences without requiring custom scripting. Visualization routines generate distribution plots, contour-density maps, multivariate embeddings, and representative shape mosaics to summarize population heterogeneity and morphological organization. Applied to pluripotent stem cell cultures subjected to chromatin perturbation, the platform detects coordinated changes in colony growth behavior and structural architecture that may not be evident through visual scoring alone. The protocol describes installation, configuration, batch image processing, quality control, hierarchical data aggregation, and downstream statistical analysis, providing a reproducible approach for transforming qualitative colony assays into quantitative, high-content phenotypic datasets suitable for stem cell research and screening applications.

items.title: Barriers to Addressing Sexual Health Needs of Adults With Chronic Kidney Disease: A Multidisciplinary Survey of Renal Healthcare Professionals.
items.authors: McKeaveney C, Sun X, McMahon J, Bonner A, Donald M, Dumanski S, Elliott M, Finderup J.
items.abstract:
Background

Sexual dysfunction is common among adults with chronic kidney disease and can significantly affect health and well-being. Understanding healthcare professionals' attitudes, training experiences, and perceived barriers toward discussing sexual health needs with patients is essential to improving patient care.

Methods

A cross-sectional survey was conducted with healthcare professionals involved in the care of adults with chronic kidney disease. The survey comprised four sections aimed to uncover participants' attitudes and beliefs toward sexual health, experience of sexual health training and practice, and barriers to discussing sexual health. Recruitment and data collection were conducted through social media and professional renal networks between December 2022 and April 2023. Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages) were employed to summarise responses. Bivariate analyses were conducted to examine differences in sexual health attitude and belief scores across participants' age, sex, and professional experience. Open-ended responses were summarised descriptively.

Results

A total of 135 participants completed the survey. Most were female nurses aged 35-54, working in haemodialysis, with more than 10 years' experience. Almost 80% had not received any sexual health training in their current or previous roles. The average attitude score was 35.49 ± 6.95, suggesting a relatively positive attitude. Ninety percent believed that addressing sexual health is essential for optimising patients' health outcomes. Key barriers included a lack of training, insufficient knowledge, and cultural or religious considerations.

Conclusion

Training for healthcare professionals on addressing sexual health in renal care is limited. Educational initiatives are required to improve professionals' confidence and competence in discussing sexual health.

items.title: Reliable identification of homodimers using AlphaFold.
items.authors: Narrowe S, Elofsson A.
items.abstract: Protein-protein interactions are central to understanding biological processes. Predicting interaction partners is extremely valuable for avoiding costly, time-consuming experiments. AlphaFold has shown an unsurpassed ability to predict protein-protein interactions accurately. However, a protein can also form homomeric interactions, that is, interact with itself. When identifying homodimers, AlphaFold yielded a significantly higher false-positive rate than when identifying heterodimers. True Positive Rate (TPR) at 1% False Positive Rate (FPR) drops from 81% for heterodimers to 22% for homodimers. When we investigated the high-scoring false positives, that is, non-homodimers with high AlphaFold scores that were predicted as such, we found that their homologs were enriched for homomultimeric proteins, indicating that stoichiometry is not always conserved among homologs. We split our dataset into a training and test set and with a simple logistic regression model that combines AlphaFold scores with stoichiometry information among homologs and interface features from the predicted structures. This logistic regression model was able to increase the performance on the test set from 27% TPR (at 1% FPR) to 36%. Without homology stoichiometry information, no improvement was seen. The higher number of high-scoring false predictions for homodimers indicates that homodimer prediction still has significant room for improvement.

items.title: Exploring the Implementation Potential of Integrating Diabetes Care Into Tuberculosis Services in Pakistan: A Qualitative Case Study.
items.authors: Afaq S, Jamal SF, Rehman A, Ashfaq U, Zala, Asim M, Khan FU, Gill S, Khan HL, Sarfraz M, Khan Z, Siddiqi K, Jennings H.
items.abstract:
Background

The co-occurrence of diabetes and tuberculosis (TB) worsens outcomes for both conditions, increasing mortality risk and treatment failure. Despite the need for integrated care for the two conditions, evidence on feasible and context-specific implementation strategies remains limited. This study explored the implementation potential of contextually designed implementation strategies to integrate diabetes within TB care in Pakistan, using the Optimised TB and Diabetes (Opt-TBD) package.

Methods

This qualitative case study was conducted from October 2023 to June 2024, across four TB facilities representing primary, secondary and tertiary levels of care in Pakistan. Using a qualitative design, we conducted in-depth interviews with TB patients with comorbid diabetes (n = 12) at 3 and 6 months after implementation, while healthcare providers (n = 6) were interviewed towards the end of the implementation period. We applied the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) alongside Proctor's implementation outcomes framework to explore implementation processes and six implementation outcomes: acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, adoption, penetration and sustainability.

Results

Several contextually tailored implementation strategies, including structured staff training, standardised screening protocols and strengthened referral mechanisms, were employed to integrate diabetes care within routine TB services. Overall, the intervention aligned well with existing TB workflows, provided that adequate resources, clearly defined referral pathways and ongoing staff training were ensured. Despite logistical challenges-such as delays in obtaining HbA1c test results and patient privacy concerns-healthcare providers reported adopting diabetes screening and counselling practices beyond the initial study participants. Strong leadership engagement and consistent programmatic support facilitated early implementation; however, sustaining these efforts long-term will require securing dedicated financial resources and formal integration into policy frameworks.

Conclusion

This qualitative study indicates promising implementation potential for integrating the Opt-TBD care package within routine TB services in Pakistan. Participants generally perceived the package as acceptable and workable within routine TB services, while laboratory delays, referral challenges and dependence on external financing remained important barriers to wider implementation. These findings informed refinement of the Opt-TBD package and the subsequent broader RE-AIM evaluation.

Lived experience or public contribution

To develop a more inclusive and contextually relevant integrated TB-diabetes care pathway, we gathered input from both service providers and service users, including patients with TB-diabetes multimorbidity. The Opt-TBD care package was co-designed with relevant stakeholders, and this qualitative study was undertaken to capture the experiences and insights of patients and healthcare providers during implementation. Participation was sought across different genders, age groups, provinces and levels of care to ensure a broad range of perspectives. This approach helped ensure that the views of those directly affected by and involved in service delivery informed the refinement of the care package and its implementation strategies.

items.title: An Evidence-Based Practice and Process Improvement Initiative Decreases Blood Culture Contamination and Healthcare Costs.
items.authors: Martini K, Heathers R, Strait LA, Beckett C.
items.abstract:
Significance and background

Blood culture contamination contributes to diagnostic errors, unnecessary antibiotic use, prolonged hospital stays, and increased healthcare costs. In 2024, a system-wide initiative was launched across a 15-hospital Midwest healthcare system to reduce contamination rates using the Practice and Process Improvement: Integrated Evidence-Based Quality (PPQ) Model, which integrates evidence-based practice (EBP) and process improvement methodologies.

Aims of the initiative

This initiative aimed to: (1) identify best practices for the reduction of blood culture contamination; (2) reduce blood culture contamination by implementing the best practice, which included standardized, evidence-based collection kits and dedicated teams to enhance team competency; and (3) establish a sustainable feedback system to support practice and continuous quality improvement.

Implementation procedure

Guided by the Advancing Research through Close Collaboration (ARCC) model and the DMAIC process, a multidisciplinary team identified best practices and practice and process gaps. Interventions included redesigning blood culture kits to integrate forcing functions and aseptic techniques, embedding multimodal education strategies, and launching a small test of change with robust leadership support. Real-time data feedback loops and unit-based contextual assessments supported sustainable implementation.

Outcomes

Post-implementation, the test unit achieved zero contaminations and zero CLABSI events over 5 months. Compliance with peripheral collection by dedicated, trained staff exceeded 98%. Projected cost avoidance included $133,500 in antibiotic use and $2.4 M from reduced length of stay. The initiative demonstrated operational feasibility, system alignment, and improved care quality.

Linking evidence to action

This project demonstrates how practice and process improvement combined with well-planned implementation leads to positive outcomes and substantial return on investment. Effective collaboration between interprofessional teams led to successful system-wide implementation, resulting in practical and sustained practice change.

items.title: Cultural safety as clinical practice: an evidence-informed model for general practice training.
items.authors: Brumpton K, Evans R, Sen Gupta T, Ward R.
items.abstract:
Background

Cultural safety is a core expectation of contemporary general practice and a critical component of high-quality care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. It is defined by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) as an ongoing, reflective practice that recognises power imbalances, addresses systemic racism, and is determined by the patient. Cultural safety remains difficult to operationalise within general practice education and assessment. Traditional training and assessment tools privilege observable behaviours and technical competence, offering limited capacity to evaluate reflexivity, power awareness, and relational trust. This study aimed to develop a community-informed framework and recommendations to guide the teaching, supervision, and assessment of cultural safety in general practice training.

Methods

A multi-phase qualitative and consensus-development study was undertaken in Australian general practice settings. Data were drawn from interviews with general practitioners (GPs), GP registrars, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander participants; a modified nominal group technique incorporating yarning with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander participants; and a modified eDelphi process involving experts in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health, education, and community leadership. Findings from all phases were synthesised and aligned with the Ahpra definition of cultural safety to develop a consolidated framework.

Results

The resulting framework articulates key knowledge domains, skills, and practising behaviours relevant to culturally safe general practice, while emphasising reflexivity, power awareness, and relational accountability. It identifies elements that may be meaningfully supported and assessed within training, highlights the central role of patient perspectives, and cautions against checklist-based approaches that risk undermining the relational nature of cultural safety.

Conclusion

This study presents a practical, evidence-informed framework and recommendations to support general practice training organisations, supervisors, and registrars in embedding cultural safety within clinical education and assessment. Grounded in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives and expert consensus, the framework offers guidance for moving beyond procedural approaches towards culturally safe practice as a relational, patient-determined process.

items.title: Supporting the Uptake of Evidence-Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory.
items.authors: O'Leary H, Toomey E, French HP, Glynn L, Robinson K, Ryan LG, Toomey C, Jenkins H, McCreesh K.
items.abstract:
Background

Management of a degenerative meniscal tear (DMT) or symptoms consistent with early knee osteoarthritis (OA) frequently deviates from international clinical practice guidelines, which recommend education and exercise as first-line treatments and strongly advise against arthroscopic partial meniscectomy. There is a need for implementation strategies to support the uptake of evidence-based care.

Methods

A systematic, four-step intervention development process was used to guide development of a multi-faceted implementation intervention targeting both individuals with a DMT or early knee OA and their general practitioners (GPs). The process integrated behavioural theory, stakeholder perspectives and evidence on intervention effectiveness. Target behaviours were identified through a literature review and stakeholder consultation. Previously conducted qualitative interviews with 17 GPs and 11 people with DMT were re-analysed and mapped to the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) to identify behavioural barriers and enablers to the targeted behaviours. Behaviour change techniques (BCTs) and intervention components were then selected to address these determinants. Stakeholder input was incorporated to enhance acceptability and feasibility.

Results

The resulting intervention aims to promote guideline-concordant management of a DMT and early knee OA. A programme theory to guide implementation was developed to describe hypothesised mechanisms of action, and candidate outcome measures were identified to support future evaluation and assess the mediating mechanisms of behaviour change.

Conclusion

Using a systematic, theory-informed and stakeholder-engaged approach, we developed a multi-faceted intervention to support delivery and uptake of evidence-based care for DMT and early knee OA. The intervention comprised GP educational workshops and resources to support an 'enhanced consultation', alongside referral to an early 'best practice' physiotherapy session. Patients received both components. The intervention was designed to be feasible, acceptable and locally relevant, but requires further testing to assess implementation and potential for scale-up in clinical practice.

Lived experience or public contribution

Stakeholder contributions played a central role in this study. People with lived experience of degenerative meniscal tears and/or knee OA (n = 6) and healthcare professional stakeholders (n = 15) were consulted during group discussions and individual meetings. Stakeholders informed every step of the development process, aiming to ensure the final intervention was feasible, acceptable and adapted to the local context.

items.title: Biosafety level-3 cryo-electron tomography of active severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 virions.
items.authors: Fukuhara H, Dokainish HM, Kita S, Tabata K, Takasu A, Huiskonen JT, Anraku Y, Nomai T, Someya T, Senda T, Stuart DI, Sasaki M, Orba Y, Suzuki Y, Sawa H, Maenaka K.
items.abstract: Understanding the structural properties of pathogenic viruses in their native, infectious state is critical for rational vaccine and drug development. However, conducting cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) under biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) containment presents significant challenges. Here, we established and validated a high-end cryo-EM workflow within a BSL-3 facility, comprehensively integrating facility design, containment measures, sample handling, cryo-transfer systems, and decontamination protocols. To demonstrate the utility and reproducibility of this workflow, we applied cryo-electron tomography to investigate severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 in its native, active state. Our observations confirm that unfixed viral particles display pleomorphic features comparable to those previously reported in fixed or inactivated preparations, validating that these structural characteristics represent native features rather than artifacts of chemical fixation. Furthermore, spatial redistribution of surface spikes was observed. The establishment of this robust BSL-3 cryo-EM workflow provides a practical blueprint for the structural characterization of emerging high-consequence pathogens, supporting pandemic preparedness, vaccine development, and antiviral discovery.

items.title: How Can We Help People With Long-Term Health Conditions Understand and Engage in Physical Activity Maintenance From Healthcare to Community Settings? Perspectives of Patients, Carers and Professionals.
items.authors: Gavin JP, Holt L, Chiu X, Dando C, McDonough S.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Physical activity (PA) is vital for managing long-term health conditions (LTCs), yet maintaining regular PA remains a global challenge. Partnerships between healthcare, leisure, and community services can provide accessible PA opportunities, but current pathways focus on initiating, rather than maintaining PA. Understanding factors influencing progression along PA pathways and engagement of professionals is essential.

Methods

Four focus groups of people with LTCs (n = 21; aged 39-82 years) were complemented by interviews with 19 professionals (aged 26-66) and five carers (aged 20-78 years). Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate understanding about recommendations for an integrated PA maintenance pathway, before mapping themes to the COM-B (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, Behaviour) model.

Results

Key themes were: i) limited access to, and information about PA services; ii) a need for improved intersectoral collaboration; and iii) opportunities and barriers to developing a PA maintenance pathway. Primary care and community centres were deemed reliable and accessible locations to advertise local opportunities, but without digital platforms, lacked recency and condition-appropriate activities. Intermediaries emerged as community navigators, working intersectorally with knowledge of local communities, and behaviour change techniques to support maintenance. However, funding cuts limited intersectoral working.

Conclusion

Maintaining PA among people with LTCs and carers requires a coordinated, intersectoral pathway between healthcare and community services, which extends beyond initial consultation and referral. Investment in collaborative infrastructure, accessible digital systems, and sustainable funding is lacking. However, community-based intermediaries trained in digital tools, can play a pivotal role in supporting maintenance by connecting individuals with appropriate opportunities and providing ongoing behaviour change.

items.title: Parent Representatives' Experiences of Participating in Children's Disability Network Team Service Improvement Groups in Ireland: A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: Moran G, O'Leary N, Robinson K, Christie H, Grant A, Garland A, Doyle E, Tomro-Hofmann R, Gallagher AL.
items.abstract:
Background

Effective patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) is an essential element of a quality healthcare system. In recent years, public health services for children with disabilities in Ireland have sought to include the voice of parent representatives in service improvement. Such initiatives provide important learning opportunities for comparable public health systems internationally.

Objective

This study aimed to explore parents' experiences of the representative role within Ireland's Children's Disability Network Teams. Understanding these experiences can inform the development and implementation of meaningful PPIE in service development in Ireland and beyond.

Design

A descriptive qualitative study was undertaken with guidance from a PPIE parent advisory group. Data were gathered via semi-structured online interviews, transcribed and analysed thematically. Findings were reviewed by the PPIE parent advisory group.

Setting and participants

Eleven participants were recruited to the study from a diverse range of health regions across Ireland. All participants had direct experience as a member of a parent representative forum related to children's disability services.

Results

Four themes were identified: (i) From the individual to the collective, parent motivations to become a representative; (ii) An ambiguous and informal role, with unintended consequences; (iii) The health system as a controlling and transactional organisation; and (iv) Unheard, unseen, and unsafe: The burden of representation.

Conclusions

Participants described experiences which reveal psychological, logistical and organisational barriers that limited the possibility of meaningful partnership and influence within service improvement processes. The findings demonstrate the importance of ensuring that the role of parent representative is clearly defined and formalised, and of the need to provide support and training around the role for parents. The study findings also highlight the importance of ensuring parents are properly recompensed for their time and efforts. Enabling parent representatives to connect informally with one another may mitigate the emotional burden of the role. More broadly, the findings suggest that meaningful partnership requires not only formal involvement structures but also transparency, trust and genuine opportunities to influence decision-making.

Lived experience

PPIE contributors collaborated in the study design and developed the interview guide, supported recruitment, contributed to interpretation and refinement of themes, informed the discussion of findings, and reviewed the final manuscript.

items.title: Focus Where It Matters: Design and Implementation of a Physiology-Based Care Pathway for Traumatic Shock.
items.authors: Noonan M, Mathew J, Hendel S, Underhill A, Miller JP, Cass A, Thomson H, Bannon-Murphy H, Fitzgerald M.
items.abstract:
Objective

Traumatic shock lacks a consensus definition, and in blunt-predominant systems its causes are heterogeneous. Simple physiological parameters remain the most universally available basis for early recognition. We describe the design and staged implementation of a physiology-based care pathway for traumatic shock and evaluate its implementation through staff experience.

Methods

Single-centre quality-improvement and implementation project at an Australian Level 1 trauma centre, reported per SQUIRE 2.0. The pathway comprised physiology-based activation (systolic blood pressure ≤ 90 mmHg, shock index > 1, prehospital blood or senior clinician concern), structured pre-arrival preparation, trauma bay and equipment standardisation, task-based team roles, prioritised life-saving interventions and senior-led disposition, supported by simulation and embedded quality improvement. Components were implemented between June and November 2022. Evaluation comprised pre-intervention (2021) and post-implementation (2025) staff surveys, summarised as top-box favourability, with cross-sectional characterisation of the shocked cohort. Clinical effectiveness was not assessed.

Results

Of 3667 major trauma patients, 324 (8.8%) met shocked trauma criteria; these patients were younger, more severely injured and had markedly higher mortality (emergency department death 6.8% vs. 0.4%). Favourable ratings of trauma bay equipment and environment rose from approximately one-quarter to 87.0%. Post-implementation, staff reported high favourability for timely life-saving interventions (88.9%), pathway embedding (85.2%) and role confidence (86.5%). Leadership clarity, communication and reliable debriefing did not improve and were identified as ongoing targets.

Conclusions

A physiology-based traumatic shock pathway was feasibly implemented and embedded, with high staff-reported readiness and clear targets for refinement. Effectiveness remains to be established.

items.title: A Qualitative Exploration of Patient and Public Involvement Experiences in Core Outcome Set Development: Insights From Public Partners and Research Stakeholders.
items.authors: Hsu S, Phadraig CMG, Scott T, Daly M, Akintola C, Geddis-Regan A.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Patient and public involvement (PPI) in research engages patients and the public in all aspects of the research process, ensuring that the perspectives of those directly affected by healthcare systems are integral to decision-making processes. PPI is recognised as central to the development of Core Outcome Sets (COS), standardised collections of outcomes that should be reported in all clinical trials. Despite agreement on the importance of PPI, limited evidence exists on the experience of PPI across partners and research stakeholders. This study explored experiences of PPI during the development of a Core Outcome Set (COS) for dental behaviour support (DBS), with recommendations for better practice.

Methods

Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured group discussions and individual interviews with PPI partners and key research stakeholders who designed, coordinated, or worked alongside the PPI process. Transcripts were analysed using iterative reflexive thematic analysis. Themes were developed and refined through continuous engagement with PPI partners, who provided feedback to shape interpretation and ensure authenticity. Data management and coding were conducted using NVivo (QSR International Pty Ltd, Version 12).

Results

Four themes captured partners' experiences of PPI within COS development. These highlighted the importance of managing expectations, creating a supportive and inclusive environment, and fostering opportunities for shared learning and reflection. Ten participants were interviewed, including PPI partners and key research stakeholders. Partners described how meaningful involvement changed their understanding of research and strengthened the partnership between researchers and the public. Practical recommendations were shared for future PPI engagement in COS studies.

Conclusion

Effective PPI in COS development requires clear role definition, inclusive collaboration, and ongoing reflexivity. A dedicated PPI Coordinator plays a vital role in supporting communication, trust, and PPI partner empowerment, ensuring participants are valued as co-developers rather than passive reviewers.

Patient and public contribution

PPI partners initiated this study, participated as interviewees, supported data interpretation, and co-authored this paper.

items.title: From Transnational Training to Local Capacity: The Sultanate of Oman-South Africa Split-Funnel Model for Genetic Counseling Workforce Development.
items.authors: van Wyk C, Bruwer Z, Al-Kharusi K, Laing N, Wessels TM.
items.abstract: As genomic technologies become increasingly integrated into healthcare worldwide, the demand for culturally and linguistically competent genetic counselors is rapidly expanding. In many regions, however, demand for these professionals far exceeds the availability of local training programs. Traditional solutions, reliance on non-local expatriate professionals or sending trainees abroad, are often costly, logistically complex, and poorly aligned with local sociocultural contexts. In the Sultanate of Oman, where high rates of consanguinity contribute to a disproportionately elevated burden of genetic and congenital disorders, the need for a locally trained workforce is particularly urgent. This descriptive professional issue report critically reflects on a transnational training model developed through a partnership among Sultan Qaboos University Hospital (SQUH), Sultan Qaboos Comprehensive Cancer Care and Research Center (SQCCCRC) in the Sultanate of Oman, and the University of Cape Town (UCT) in South Africa to address these structural gaps. The model, conceptualized as a "Split-Funnel Model," integrates international academic training with sustained, supervised in-country clinical practice. Trainees completed intensive academic blocks and clinical training at UCT while delivering clinical care in Oman, an arrangement intended to support the development of clinical expertise and culturally grounded practice. A central feature of this model is "system code-switching," defined as the adaptation of Western-derived counseling frameworks to culturally responsive, collectivist, and family-centered healthcare contexts. During the model's operation, Oman's genetic counseling workforce and service capacity expanded from a single non-Omani-led clinic to three national centers staffed by five qualified Omani genetic counselors; however, the descriptive design does not establish that the training model caused this growth. This experience suggests that a distributed transnational approach may be feasible and potentially valuable for developing a culturally competent genetic counseling workforce without established local academic infrastructure. Even though the report is based on retrospective programmatic observations of five trainees within one partnership, it does not establish the model's effectiveness, scalability, or transferability. However, the model may still offer practical guidance for countries seeking to build a locally embedded genetic counseling workforce before establishing an independent domestic training program.

items.title: A linear-transformer hybrid for single-nucleotide polymorphism-based genotype-to-phenotype prediction in grapevine.
items.authors: Wang Y, Jayakodi M, Kirubakaran S, Chandra A, Zahid A.
items.abstract: Robust genotype-to-phenotype (G2P) prediction is essential for accelerating grapevine (Vitis spp.) breeding decisions and genetic gain. However, it remains challenging to measure complex traits under variable field conditions and across years. In this study, we propose a linear-Transformer (LiT)-G2P, an automated predictive framework that integrates additive genetic variance effects with Transformer-based nonlinear interactions using genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) data. We evaluated LiT-G2P on a panel of diverse grape accessions, genotyped with SNP markers and measured for phenotypes across three consecutive years. Target phenotypic traits include leaf hair density and trichome density of grapevines. Across both single-year and cross-year testing scenarios, LiT-G2P consistently improves prediction performance compared with baseline models. For leaf hair density, LiT-G2P achieved the lowest prediction errors in both single-year and cross-year evaluations, with root mean square error (RMSE) values of 0.475 and 0.460 and ± 0.5 accuracies of 78.6% and 72.9%, respectively. For trichome density, LiT-G2P achieved RMSE values of 0.637 and 0.766 and corresponding accuracies of 62.6% and 58.2%. In addition, we extracted model-prioritized SNPs from attention weights and applied genotype-stratified analysis to provide interpretable candidate marker for downstream validation. These results support practical SNP-based predictive modeling for genomic selection and identify the remaining need for more detailed field data, larger multi-year grapevine panels, and independent grapevine validation before broader deployment.

items.title: Digital Follow-Up After Total Knee Arthroplasty: An Interview Study Among Orthopaedic Surgeons.
items.authors: Craamer C, Timmers T, Weegen WV, Kool RB.
items.abstract:
Background

Traditionally, patients who undergo total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are scheduled for an in-person routine follow-up (RFU) regimen. Increasing pressure on orthopaedic services and growing acceptance of digital health technologies urge clinics to adopt more efficient RFU strategies. However, limited insight exists into how RFU after TKA is organised in clinical practice and under which conditions digital follow-up is acceptable to orthopaedic surgeons. This study explored current RFU practices after TKA and examined surgeons' perspectives on digital follow-up.

Methods

A qualitative study using semi-structured interviews was conducted with 21 orthopaedic surgeons from different healthcare institutions. Interviews were conducted digitally, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using qualitative analysis software. Two researchers independently coded the transcripts, after which the codes were compared, refined, and grouped into overarching themes.

Results

Four main themes emerged. (1) RFU after TKA was highly fragmented across institutions, with variation in timing, contact modality, responsible healthcare provider, and use of radiographic assessment. (2) Follow-up visits were primarily perceived as a means to confirm uncomplicated recovery and detect complications early. (3) Digital follow-up was viewed not as a replacement for in-person visits but as an additional triage strategy to support decisions on physical consultation. (4) Acceptance of digital follow-up depended on clear patient selection, predefined clinical recovery indicators, and preservation of professional and patient autonomy.

Conclusion

RFU after TKA is poorly standardized and institution dependent. Digital follow-up is considered acceptable mainly as a triage mechanism if patient safety, professional autonomy, and the surgeon-patient relationship are maintained.

items.title: Nursing Student Led Blood Pressure Education in a Community Mental Health Setting: A Pre Post Test Study.
items.authors: Stephen C, Yousiph T, Halcomb E, Jay EK, Smith B, Patterson C, Curtis E, Mullan J, Moxham L.
items.abstract: People living with mental illness have greater cardiovascular risk, more lifestyle risk factors and lower health literacy than the general population. The high prevalence of hypertension among people living with mental illness places them at a significantly higher risk of premature morbidity and mortality. Identifying hypertension and empowering consumers to understand its significance are key to controlling elevated blood pressure. Student nurse led blood pressure education in community mental health settings may improve hypertension awareness while building nursing students' confidence and competence. This study sought to evaluate the impact of a preregistration nursing student led blood pressure education activity on consumer blood pressure knowledge and nursing students' health education competence. A single group pre post test intervention study was undertaken during a community mental health clinical placement (Recovery Camp, New South Wales, Australia). Nursing students delivered a brief blood pressure education activity to consumers living with mental illness. Consumer knowledge was assessed using the Hypertension Evaluation of Lifestyle and Management (HELM) scale, and student competence was assessed using the Nurse Health Education Competence Instrument (I-CEpSE). Twenty-one consumers completed paired assessments. Mean HELM scores increased from 5.0 (SD 2.65) pre activity to 6.9 (SD 2.69) post activity (p < 0.001). Forty-four students completed paired assessments, with I-CEpSE total scores increasing from 210.95 (SD 28.81) to 257.27 (SD 30.22) (p < 0.001). This study has demonstrated that a structured, student led blood pressure education activity embedded within a community mental health placement improved both consumer hypertension knowledge and student reported health education competence.

items.title: Research Priorities for Preconception Health in Scotland: A Multidisciplinary Call to Action.
items.authors: Currie S, Brough EJ, Ryan L, Renwick K, Rose B, Ganguly A.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Health and behaviours prior to conception influence reproductive outcomes, lifelong health, and health inequalities across generations. While international attention to preconception health has increased, context-specific evidence to inform effective practice and policy in Scotland remains limited. This gap is concerning given declining birth rates, widening inequalities, and increasing prevalence of adverse maternal and infant outcomes.

Methods

A research prioritisation project was undertaken to identify key areas for preconception health research in Scotland. A narrative review of published literature reviews and relevant Scottish policy and public health guidance was conducted to identify evidence gaps and preliminary research themes. These informed a national online survey that captured views from members of the public and stakeholders with an interest in preconception health. Survey findings were subsequently refined through an in-person, multi-stakeholder workshop involving members of the public, researchers, healthcare professionals, third sector representatives, and policy stakeholders.

Results

Four overarching research priority themes were identified: (1) adopting a life-course approach to preconception health; (2) reducing neurodevelopmental risks and improving awareness of preconception behaviours; (3) addressing health inequalities and ensuring equitable access to care; and (4) enhancing the involvement of men, partners, and shared responsibility for preconception health. Cross-cutting principles emphasised the need for inclusive and consistent messaging, improved healthcare professional training, integration of preconception care within existing services, stakeholder involvement, and robust data collection.

Conclusion

This co-designed research prioritisation project identifies clear and actionable priorities for advancing preconception health research in Scotland. Addressing these priorities will support evidence-based policy and practice, improve reproductive and long-term health outcomes, and contribute to reducing health inequalities for current and future generations.

Public contribution

Members of the public and individuals with lived experience of preconception health were actively involved throughout this research prioritisation project. Public contributors participated in a national survey to identify and rank priorities for preconception health research in Scotland and attended a multi-stakeholder workshop to refine and finalise research themes and questions. The workshop included members of the public alongside researchers, healthcare professionals, third sector representatives, and policy stakeholders, ensuring that priorities reflected lived experience as well as professional perspectives. Public input directly informed the identification of research priorities, the interpretation of findings, and the development of future research directions (See the GRIPP2 short form checklist in the supplementary files).

items.title: Accessing and Navigating Gender-Affirming Hormone Therapy and Perspectives on Inclusive Pharmacy Care Among Transgender and Gender Diverse People: A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: McCann J, Wilcock S, Dominy I, Davison K, Sharman S, Robinson-Barella A.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Transgender and gender diverse (TGD) people continue to experience inequities in access to gender-affirming care, including stigmatisation, delayed treatment and non-inclusive healthcare encounters. Community pharmacies may represent an accessible setting to support inclusive and affirming care; however, lived experiences of engaging with community pharmacy services in the context of gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) remain underexplored, particularly among younger people who represent the greatest proportion of the TGD community. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of accessing, navigating and receiving GAHT, alongside participants' perspectives on barriers and facilitators to accessing inclusive and affirming care within community pharmacy.

Methods

Semi-structured interviews were conducted between October and November 2025. Interviews explored participant experiences of accessing GAHT and perspectives on inclusive and affirming pharmacy practice. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. NVivo (Version 15) facilitated data management, and the COREQ and CCRF checklists informed reporting. Ethical approval was obtained from the Newcastle University Research Ethics Committee (reference: 66105/2023).

Results

Ten participants, representing a range of gender identities, were interviewed. Three overarching themes were developed: (1) reflecting on the challenges of navigating gender-affirming hormone therapy; (2) exploring the impact of healthcare barriers upon an individual and (3) accessing and receiving inclusive and affirming pharmacy care. Participants viewed community pharmacies as accessible and supportive environments for affirming care when underpinned by respectful communication, visible inclusivity, appropriate staff training and partnership working with TGD communities.

Conclusion

In this study, TGD individuals described significant structural and interpersonal barriers when accessing GAHT in the United Kingdom, negatively influencing trust, wellbeing and engagement with healthcare services. Community pharmacies may represent an underutilised, yet important, setting for inclusive and gender-affirming support. Embedding gender-affirming training and co-designed approaches within pharmacy services may strengthen accessibility, trust and equity in care for TGD communities.

Lived experience or public contribution

A person with lived experience from the TGD community (ID) acted as a co-author and patient champion in this study; they supported the design and conduct of the research, advised on inclusive and non-stigmatising approaches and supported preparation of the manuscript, contributing a lived-experience perspective throughout.

items.title: Implementation and Performance of a Clinical Debriefing Programme in a Paediatric Emergency Department: A Descriptive Qualitative Review.
items.authors: Reeves KL, Batty A, Plummer K.
items.abstract:
Objective

Clinical debriefing should be standard practice in healthcare, but in most emergency departments implementation lags behind evidence. This post-implementation evaluation examined the performance of a clinical debriefing programme in a tertiary care paediatric emergency department, exploring implementation, key enablers and barriers to use.

Methods

This qualitative descriptive, post-implementation study used semi-structured interviews, with deductive analysis guided by a context-mechanism-outcome framework.

Results

Twenty-one multidisciplinary staff were interviewed. Debriefing became embedded in routine practice through organisational endorsement, structured facilitation and inclusive participation. Participants reported improved clinical reasoning, emotional regulation, psychological safety and interprofessional relationships. Debriefing strengthened support for junior staff, enhanced relational co-ordination across disciplines, facilitated more timely quality and safety actions and built nursing capacity to lead debriefs. Time was the principal barrier, but reframing debriefing as an integral component of clinical care enabled its routine delivery.

Conclusions

Clinical debriefing was embedded in routine practice through interactions between organisational context and implementation mechanisms, with successful implementation relying on both the intervention and the conditions enabling it. Benefits for clinical practice, staff well-being, teamwork, enhanced support for the junior workforce and timely quality improvement initiatives were described. This study advances current understanding and provides direction for teams seeking to implement or optimise debriefing within their own departments.

items.title: Time, Trust and Participation: A Nationwide Quantitative Study of Person-Centred Care in Forensic Mental Health Settings.
items.authors: Vidaurrázaga Aras V, Wolf A, Nilsson T, Alexiou E, Olausson S.
items.abstract: Person-centred care emphasises the uniqueness of individuals through partnerships, the co-creation of care plans and coordinated health care. Its implementation in forensic mental health services is challenged by legal coercion and restrictive practices. Person-centred principles are embedded in legislation; however, national data on patients' perspectives on person-centred care are lacking. This study aimed to map person-centred care as perceived by patients and to identify areas for improvement. A nationwide survey included 329 patients across 13 forensic psychiatric hospitals in Sweden using the Generic Person-Centred Care Questionnaire supplemented with contextual background questions. The median Generic Person-Centred Care Questionnaire score was 70 (range 19-95). Length of stay was associated with perceived person-centred care; patients hospitalised for 2-5 years reported higher total scores than those hospitalised for more than 10 years, although the pairwise difference did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Trust in staff differed by length of stay, with patients hospitalised for > 10 years reporting significantly lower trust than those hospitalised for 0-1 and 2-5 years. Communicative safety showed a similar pattern, although pairwise differences were not significant after correction. No significant differences in total scores were found by gender, age, ethnicity, diagnosis, or hospital type. Overall, patients reported positive experiences of respect and emotional support. Among those who reported having a written care plan, involvement in and understanding of the plan were rated positively, whereas broader involvement in decision-making, use of patients' own resources and relatives' participation received lower ratings, indicating areas for further improvement in person-centred practice.

items.title: Astrocytic EAAT-2 Upregulation Supports Neuro-Axonal Homeostasis in Chronic Inflammatory CNS Lesions.
items.authors: Reukauf L, Margineanu A, Muinjonov B, Chen J, Cui Y, Rosiewicz K, Radbruch H, Munro I, Alisch M, Siffrin V.
items.abstract: Neuronal loss in multiple sclerosis (MS) is a key factor in the progression of disability. Axonal degeneration within MS lesions is central to progressive MS pathology, yet its mechanisms are not fully understood. Excess extracellular l-glutamate (GLUT) is neurotoxic due to overstimulation of GLUT receptors. Excitotoxicity, driven by GLUT, is a suspected contributor to several central nervous system (CNS) diseases. Astrocytic glutamate transporters EAAT-1 and EAAT-2 play crucial roles in managing extracellular GLUT, yet their role in chronic MS remains underexplored. Using the animal model experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and advanced microscopy in live anesthetized mice, we examined GLUT-mediated neurotoxicity and protective mechanisms in chronic CNS lesions. By employing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors, we visualized extracellular GLUT levels and axonal Ca<sup>2+</sup> dynamics within the live mouse brain during EAE. In acute EAE, extracellular GLUT levels were high, while in chronic lesions, normalized GLUT levels together with sustained EAAT-2 upregulation were consistent with a protective astrocytic response. EAAT-2 inhibition in chronic lesions led to higher intra-axonal Ca<sup>2+</sup> levels and morphological changes consistent with neuroaxonal injury, indicating that EAAT-2 upregulation may counter excitotoxicity and support neuroprotection. Post-mortem MS brain tissue analysis provided complementary evidence, showing elevated EAAT-1 and EAAT-2 expression in chronic MS lesions with expression patterns varying according to lesion type and cellularity. This study highlights astrocytic mechanisms that may contribute to neuroaxonal protection in MS tissue and suggests targeting GLUT transporters as a promising strategy to limit neurodegeneration in progressive MS.

items.title: Working Right Ways: Investigating Health Practitioners' Perspectives of Foot Health and Needs for Providing Good Foot Care With and for First Nations Peoples.
items.authors: Gerrard J, Godwin Badimaya Yamatji S, Whiteley Wiradjuri K, Charles Kaurna J, Chuter V.
items.abstract:
Background

History of invasion, ongoing colonisation, and systemic racism excluding First Nations Peoples from healthcare are root causes of health inequalities including disparities in foot health outcomes. Sources of inquiry into current practice, learning, and experience, which may shape reform of providing good foot care with and for First Nations Peoples in the land now known as Australia are health practitioners working in the space. This work seeks to explore foot care service delivery by investigating First Nations and non-Indigenous health practitioners' perspectives regarding providing foot care with and for First Nations Peoples.

Methods

Ways of working are documented in previous work; 'Working right ways in foot health with and for First Nations Peoples: research method guided and governed by First Nations ways of knowing, being, and doing in cross-sectional qualitative study design'. First Nations and non-Indigenous health practitioners provided perspectives with culturally responsive semi-structured interviews guiding talking with consenting participants. Coding utilised constant comparison techniques to explore patterns across the dataset. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results

Two talking points engaged health practitioners' perspectives of providing foot care with and for First Nations Peoples: (1) What does foot health mean to you as a First Nations or non-Indigenous health practitioner? (2) What are needs for providing good foot care with and for First Nations Peoples? Within responses, themes emerged of mobility and participation, overall health and wellbeing, clinical and biomedical perspective, and advocacy being related to the meaning of foot health. The requirements of cultural safety, workforce, and holistic care were perceived as needed for provision of good foot care with and for First Nations Peoples.

Conclusion

Participants described a meaning of foot health that is relational to physical and spiritual constructs, and central to reclamation of, and continuation of, First Nations cultures; amidst a project of ongoing colonisation. Needs for good foot care provision with and for First Nations Peoples included a workforce continually learning and unlearning to develop cultural capabilities to work with and for, and support, First Nations foot health. This study provides distinct and real first-hand accounts from health practitioners working in the space which the podiatry profession must listen to and receive direction and learning from.

items.title: An Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer for Participant-Level Classification of Depressive Symptoms From Resting-State EEG.
items.authors: Ramaiah P, Nomani I, Asfour HI, Baig MR, Yuldashev M, Sapaev I, Bani Younes ZB, Sharma S, Manchanda M, Khasawneh MAS, Jabir MS.
items.abstract:
Background

Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive modality for investigating depressive symptoms; however, conventional deep-learning methods often require large labeled datasets and provide limited interpretability. We developed an Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer Network for participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG.

Methods

The framework employed masked temporal modeling for self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Model performance was evaluated using repeated nested participant-wise cross-validation and compared with conventional machine-learning and deep-learning baselines. Explainability was investigated through transformer attention maps and SHAP-based channel attribution.

Results

The proposed model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73-0.90), a precision-recall AUC of 0.69, balanced accuracy of 0.75, sensitivity of 0.72, and specificity of 0.78. The positive predictive value was 0.57, indicating a substantial false-positive burden in the evaluated cohort. The proposed model showed the highest point-estimate ROC-AUC among the evaluated baselines, with a 0.07 improvement over EEGNet; however, the overlapping uncertainty intervals and the small elevated-symptom cohort warrant cautious interpretation of comparative superiority. Performance decreased from an ROC-AUC of 0.82 in Run 1 to 0.78 in Run 2 and to 0.72-0.73 under cross-condition transfer, supporting interpretation of these analyses as internal reproducibility and condition-shift assessments rather than independent external validation. Removing self-supervised pretraining reduced the ROC-AUC to 0.74. Explainability analyses identified distributed temporally relevant intervals and frontal-midline to centro-parietal channel contributions, with attribution interpreted as model-relevance evidence rather than causal biomarker evidence.

Conclusion

Overall, the findings provide preliminary internal evidence that self-supervised temporal representation learning can support participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG under the evaluated experimental conditions. The findings do not establish clinical diagnostic validity, screening readiness, or independent external generalizability.

items.title: Concordance of Microbiological and Histopathological Examination of Bone Biopsies in Diagnosing Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis, a Systematic Review.
items.authors: Kadiri L, Maher A, Bridgen A.
items.abstract:
Background

Diabetic foot osteomyelitis (DFO) is a serious complication of diabetic foot ulcers and is associated with increased risk of amputation, morbidity, and mortality. Bone biopsy remains the most definitive diagnostic modality, yet controversy persists over its diagnostic utility This study reviews the diagnostic concordance of histopathology and microbiology in bone biopsy specimens from patients with DFO and examines the clinical implications of the findings.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted using PubMed, Medline, CINHAL, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Studies included adult patients with DFO in whom bone biopsy specimens underwent both histopathological and microbiological analysis. Five core studies met the eligibility criteria. Data on study design, setting, population, diagnostic methods, concordance rates, and outcomes were extracted and synthesized utilising a quantitative narrative synthesis.

Results

Across the five studies (n = 308 patients), histopathology and microbiology showed modest concordance, with mean rates of concordant positive results of 43.4% and common discordant findings. Histopathology demonstrated higher specificity, while microbiology had higher sensitivity, ranging from 70% to 83.9% but greater susceptibility to contamination. Positive histopathology was more strongly associated with the need for revision surgery or extended antibiotic therapy.

Discussion

Histopathology appears to offer superior diagnostic specificity, whereas microbiology provides valuable information for antimicrobial management. Frequent discordance underscores the importance of interpreting results in a clinical context. Further robust, prospective studies are needed to clarify the optimal diagnostic approach and standardise definitions.

items.title: Evaluation of voice features using Wav2vec2.0-based deep learning as a diagnostic tool in acromegaly.
items.authors: Aksoy S, Saygili ES, Akyel S, Onur O, Niyazoglu M, Hatipoglu E.
items.abstract: Acromegaly has an insidious onset and prolonged diagnostic delay. Vocal changes are a recognized clinical feature, the diagnostic value of deep learning architectures remains underexplored. We aimed to assess Wav2Vec2.0-based voice analysis as a non-invasive digital biomarker for acromegaly. This single-center case-control study included 70 patients with acromegaly and 68 age- and sex-matched controls. Clinical status was defined by standard biochemical criteria, symptoms, comorbidities, and residual tumor. Voice samples were recorded with a standard mobile phone and resampled to 16 kHz. Wav2Vec2.0 was used to extract high-dimensional embedding vectors. These embeddings, were used to train and validate four different machine learning classifiers using an 80%/20% train-test split with five-fold cross-validation. Model calibration was assessed with the Brier score, and clinical utility with decision curve analysis (DCA). Demographics were similar between acromegaly (mean age 45.5 years; 57.1% female) and control (mean age 47.5 years; 61.8% female) groups. On the internal hold-out test set, Logisitic Regression model maintained high accuracy (AUC 0.84; specificity 0.92; sensitivity 0.71) and showed good calibration [Brier score 0.165 (95% CI 0.057-0.289)]. DCA confirmed that LR provided the highest benefit across a clinically relevant range of threshold probabilities (~ 15-85%). Voice analysis Wav2Vec2.0-based model demonstrates good diagnostic accuracy for acromegaly. These preliminary findings suggest that voice may serve as a promising non-invasive digital biomarker, pending validation in larger and more diverse cohorts.

items.title: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation
items.authors: Zhu J, Yeh F, Zheng J, He Y.
items.abstract: ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-ExperimentAssay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccinerelated study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes.
