These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Embodied Artificial Intelligence with Hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control for Resilient Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
items.authors: Rahmani B, Afghah F.
items.abstract: Embodied artificial intelligence (Embodied AI) has rapidly emerged as a fundamental paradigm for developing autonomous robotic systems capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting within complex physical environments. Recent advances in foundation models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures have significantly improved high-level semantic reasoning for robotics; however, their deployment in real-world field environments remains limited by distributional shifts, multimodal uncertainty, dynamic environmental changes, and the absence of safety-aware decision-making mechanisms. These challenges become substantially more pronounced in heterogeneous multi-robot systems operating under partial observability and communication constraints. This paper presents an uncertainty-aware embodied AI framework that integrates multimodal perception, shared latent world modelling, predictive uncertainty estimation, online self-supervised representation adaptation, and hierarchical decision-making through hybrid Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control (RL-MPC). Unlike conventional embodied AI architectures that execute fixed perception and control pipelines, the proposed framework continuously maintains and updates an internal world representation, enabling adaptive reasoning, uncertainty-aware planning, and safe real-time control. Furthermore, the architecture naturally extends to heterogeneous teams of aerial robots, autonomous ground vehicles, and mobile manipulators through distributed latent representations that support cooperative perception, coordinated task allocation, and resilient autonomous behavior. The proposed framework is evaluated in photorealistic NVIDIA Isaac Sim environments containing randomized terrain geometry, vegetation density, illumination changes, dynamic obstacles, sensor degradation, communication uncertainty, and severe out-of-distribution conditions representative of realistic field robotic deployments. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over vision-based navigation, reinforcement learning, model predictive control, and hybrid RL-MPC baselines. The proposed method achieves approximately 21% higher navigation success, reduces collision frequency by more than 35%, exhibits significantly improved robustness under increasing environmental uncertainty, and maintains stable cooperative performance across heterogeneous multi-robot teams. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware embodied world models, continual representation learning, hierarchical VLA-guided decision making, and hybrid learning-control architectures provide a scalable foundation for resilient embodied intelligence and represent a promising direction toward next-generation autonomous robotic systems operating safely and reliably in complex real-world environments.

items.title: AI-Based Scenario Generation in Cyber Training Ranges: A Systematic Review
items.authors: Mehta P, Black P, Karmakar G, Pang P.
items.abstract: Developing realistic scenarios for Cyber Training Ranges (CTRs) requires current threat information, suitable infrastructure, attack events, learning objectives, and consideration of trainee capability. Established scenario-generation approaches use manual design, simulation, templates, rules, attack graphs, and model-driven engineering, often requiring substantial expert effort to develop and update. Recent research has investigated Artificial Intelligence (AI) for scenario generation and training, including Machine Learning (ML), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing surveys provide fragmented coverage of AI across the scenario-generation lifecycle and have not systematically examined AI-specific threat intelligence, such as MITRE ATLAS, as a dedicated source for CTR scenarios. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of embedding AI into CTR scenario generation, tracing the progression from non-AI approaches to ML, LLM-based, and agentic AI methods. It critically compares their advantages and limitations and examines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), agentic approaches, and AI threat intelligence-based attack scenarios. The literature indicates that AI can support scenario creation, automation, adaptation, and deployment, while important challenges remain in threat-data quality and currency, hallucinations, technical validation, reproducibility, interoperability, and alignment with training objectives. The review identifies these limitations and discusses research directions for more realistic, adaptable, and technically reliable cybersecurity training scenarios.

items.title: Distinct convective precipitation structures underlie similar surface rainfall and regional contrasts in rainfall extremes
items.authors: Wang Z, Hu X, Ai W, Zhang W, Ma S, peng H, Tan Z.
items.abstract: Conditioning radar profiles on near-surface rain rates and drop size distributions (DSDs) often obscures distinct convective structures. Instead, this study applies representation-learning-guided clustering to reflectivity-profile shapes from 1.65 million convective profiles observed by the Global Precipitation Measurement Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar, identifying six structural archetypes without near-surface inputs. They span shallow warm-rain to deep convection but overlap in near-surface precipitation properties. Despite this similarity, echo-top heights within the modal DSD bin differ threefold, reflecting contrasting ice-phase and warm-rain contributions. Across rainfall rates, these microphysical pathways diverge primarily at moderate intensities, where shallow archetypes show greater warm-layer rain-rate and drop-size increases, but converge at higher intensities as deeper archetypes show stronger drop-size growth. At the regional scale, this classification separates tropical land–ocean extreme-rainfall contrasts into opposing contributions from archetype prevalence and within-archetype extreme-rainfall probability. These findings provide structure-resolved benchmarks for evaluating convective precipitation in weather and climate models.

items.title: Disability-Inclusive HIV Service Delivery: A Participatory Mixed-Methods Study of Stakeholder-Identified Barriers and Solutions
items.authors: ONYEKWELU AI, FATAI KE, ILONDU UC.
items.abstract: Background People with disabilities may experience barriers to HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and related services. However, evidence on stakeholder-identified barriers, priorities, and solutions for disability-inclusive HIV service delivery remains limited. This study explored stakeholder perspectives on disability-inclusive HIV services, with particular attention to women and girls with disabilities. Methods A participatory mixed-methods design was used during a four-day stakeholder-engagement programme at the AIDS 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Participants engaged in five activities: SEE HER, HEAR WITH HER, DESIGN WITH HER, STAND WITH HER, and WHO IS MISSING IN HIV CARE. Structured responses were analysed descriptively using frequencies and percentages, while open-ended responses were analysed thematically. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated using a convergence approach. Results In STAND WITH HER, stigma and discrimination were the most frequently identified barrier (14/20, 70.0%), followed by lack of disability-inclusive HIV information (10/20, 50.0%) and limited availability of disability-inclusive services (9/20, 45.0%). In HEAR WITH HER, 50/51 (98.0%) classified disability inclusion across the HIV care continuum as reality, while 49/49 (100.0%) recognised that inequalities may remain unnoticed without disability-disaggregated data. In WHO IS MISSING IN HIV CARE, women and girls were the most frequently identified underrepresented population (38/118, 32.2%), followed by LGBTQI + and transgender populations and children, adolescents and young people (30/118, 25.4% each). Government was the most frequently identified actor responsible for addressing barriers (7/20, 35.0%). Qualitative and co-design findings highlighted accessible communication, provider preparedness, physical and digital accessibility, inclusive programme design, autonomy, privacy, and meaningful participation. Conclusion Stakeholders characterised disability-inclusive HIV service delivery as a multilevel issue involving stigma, accessibility, provider practices, programme design, data systems, participation, and intersecting vulnerabilities. The findings support embedding accessible communication, disability-responsive monitoring, inclusive service design, provider preparedness, and meaningful involvement of people with disabilities within routine HIV programming.

items.title: Strategies to improve engagement and inclusion of participants from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities in research involving patient-reported outcomes (PROs)
items.authors: Mercieca-Bebber R, Chong J, Tan A, Naher S, Heuschkel M, El-Kabbout N, Duan H, Stanoevska B, Stockler M.
items.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to identify barriers, facilitators and resources currently used to engage participants from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities in studies with patient-reported outcome (PRO). Methods Australian researchers or health professionals using PROs in research or clinical practice were eligible to participate in an anonymous online survey. Quantitative data was summarised descriptively; qualitative data was analysed using critical content analysis. Results Forty-eight respondents were included in the analysis (56% female, 48% academic role). Common barriers included: lack of resources to translate study materials (77%) or to offer non-English questionnaires online (70%); tight funding deadlines (64%) and budgets (61%) precluding implementation of supports; and additional administrative work (59%). Inclusion strategies included engaging consumer advocates (85%), seeking advice from experienced colleagues (71%) and directly asking participants about support needs (63%). Seventy-three percent had participated in cultural sensitivity training. Respondents estimated a median of 1.5 hours and $300 per non-English-speaking participant, and 55 hours and $20,000 per study, would be required to adequately resource these supports, although estimates varied greatly. Conclusions Despite high cultural-sensitivity awareness and uptake of inclusion and engagement strategies, clear funding and time barriers were acknowledged, reflecting that community involvement, translation of study materials, collaborative study design, and implementing ongoing supports are resource-intensive endeavours. As Australia’s CALD population continues to grow, funding bodies and research sponsors should support these needs by embedding dedicated funding, flexible timelines, and cultural safety frameworks to ensure genuine equity and inclusion of CALD communities in PRO research.

items.title: Leveraging amino acid embeddings for accurate translation efficiency prediction.
items.authors: Terai G, Asai K.
items.abstract:
Motivation

Accurate prediction of translation efficiency from mRNA sequences is an important step toward mRNA sequence design. In recent years, the widespread adoption of high-resolution ribosome profiling techniques, such as Ribo-seq, has led to rapid accumulation of large-scale datasets that capture the relationship between mRNA sequences and translation efficiency. This progress has facilitated the development of machine-learning-based models for translation efficiency prediction. However, most existing approaches rely primarily on mRNA-derived features, such as codon usage frequency and 5' untranslated regions (5'UTRs), and do not directly utilize the amino-acid-level information.

Results

In this study, we show that incorporating distributed representations (embeddings) of amino acid sequences translated from mRNA as model features can improve translation efficiency prediction. By combining fixed amino acid embeddings derived from a pretrained protein language model with mRNA-derived features, the proposed model integrates complementary protein-level and nucleotide-level information for more accurate prediction of translation efficiency.

Availability and implementation

Codes are available at GitHub (https://github.com/gterai/AA_emb) and Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23968476).

items.title: Advancing Representation of LGBTQ+, Black Immigrant, and Rural Communities in Oncology Clinical Trials: Future Considerations.
items.authors: Carter-Bawa L, George S, Krieger J, Shoulders EN.
items.abstract: Clinical trials play a major role in advances in cancer prevention, detection, treatment, and survivorship. However, clinical trials do not often include adequate representation from the populations most at risk for developing and dying from cancer, thus limiting the generalizability of trial findings. Gaining a better understanding of the barriers that limit representation in trials is essential to developing and testing interventions to overcome these barriers. This paper examines barriers to cancer clinical trial participation among LGBTQ+ people, Black immigrants, and people living in rural communities, and highlights promising strategies to advance improvements in cancer-related health outcomes for all populations. Drawing on proceedings from the 2024 Science of Community Outreach and Engagement (SoCOE) Conference, we propose actionable recommendations for embedding equity into clinical trial design, policy, and practice to ensure that all communities benefit from innovations in cancer care.

items.title: Implementing HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among cisgender female sex workers: A worldwide scoping review to guide the future research agenda for HIV prevention.
items.authors: Plazy M, Becquet V, Amador-Paz S, Nouaman M, Maouhoub E, Meertens C, Mouquin R, Youssoufa H, Coffie P, Larmarange J.
items.abstract: Female sex workers (FSWs) experience a disproportionately high burden of HIV. To inform future research and policy efforts on HIV prevention, this study synthesizes global evidence on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among cisgender FSWs worldwide. This scoping review was conducted using six multidisciplinary databases searched up to December 2024. Titles and abstracts, then full texts, were independently screened. Data extraction comprised i) general study characteristics (UNAIDS region, country, study type, outcomes, type of PrEP, and study years), ii) detailed data of each outcome (including PrEP knowledge, a priori acceptability - interest, and effective acceptability - use, retention and adherence). Drivers and barriers to PrEP acceptability were analyzed using an adapted conceptual framework encompassing six domains: patient characteristics, individual knowledge and perceptions, medication-related factors, social processes, structural and health system factors, and sex work characteristics. After selection, 120 eligible studies were identified, mostly conducted in Eastern and Southern Africa. PrEP knowledge was initially low but increased quickly once programs were introduced. PrEP interest was consistently high across regions, driven by perceived HIV risk and desire for self‑protection. PrEP uptake, retention and adherence varied widely. Main barriers included sex work realities (i.e., unstable housing, alcohol use), social processes (i.e., stigma), individual characteristics (i.e., mobility), treatment-related characteristics (i.e., side effects), and health system challenges (i.e., clinic access constraints). Drivers included social support and reminder tools. While evidence on long‑acting PrEP remained limited, interest was consistently high as reducing daily burden. Overall, the findings support a socio-ecological understanding of PrEP engagement among FSWs, including the sex work context as a distinct intermediary layer. They highlight the need for differentiated and structurally responsive PrEP delivery models tailored to the realities of sex work. Expanding long‑acting PrEP options and improving service accessibility, community engagement, and stigma reduction strategies will be critical to strengthening HIV prevention among FSWs globally.

items.title: Integrating Cost Considerations into HIV Care and Prevention to Achieve Population-Level Outcomes.
items.authors: Golden MR, Cannon CA, Menza TW, Sharma M, Porter KM, Dombrowski JC.
items.abstract: The US government currently spends >$29 billion annually on HIV treatment, but only 69% of people with diagnosed HIV (PWH) in the US are virally suppressed, a failure partially related to poverty. Medical providers preferentially treat HIV using higher cost medications, and use of higher cost drugs for PrEP is increasing. New, long-acting antiretrovirals (ARVs) have the potential to improve prevention and care while further increasing costs. We believe that the US approach to HIV should change to increase the use of lower cost HIV medications and promote the selective use of long-acting ARVs to treat people who cannot achieve viral suppression using oral drugs. A portion of the money saved through more efficient medication utilization management should be used to improve access to care and provide socioeconomic support to low-income PWH. Together, these changes have the potential to decrease costs, improve health outcomes, and better align spending with patient preferences.

items.title: A Computational Theory of Education for Human Flourishing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.authors: Wang H.
items.abstract: Generative AI now performs tasks long treated as markers of human cognitive distinctiveness. This does not make education obsolete; it makes the question of what education is for more urgent. This article develops a Computational Theory of Education for Human Flourishing in the AI Era (CTE-HF-AI) that formalizes education's role in cultivating human flourishing as its root objective, and specifies the cultivation of ethically competent, relationally present, and existentially grounded persons as education's developmental target, while treating AI as a bounded and accountable partner. The theory is a domain-specific instantiation of Constrained Object Hierarchies (COH), the general mathematical theory of intelligence developed in the MDPI Computers paper and its preprints' foundations. The theory's organizing logic is named the Flourishing-Competence-Preparation (FCP) Principle; flourishing names education's aim, ethical competence names the developmental construct through which that aim is educationally approached, and dual preparation names the design principle that operationalizes the construct. The FCP Principle is design-theoretic and normative rather than descriptive. Formally, an educational system is \(\mathcal{E} = \langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{O} \rangle\), where \(\delta\) is a bounded, uncertainty-annotated learner state. All nine COH components are instantiated: the component hierarchy \(\mathcal{C}\) is the FCP structure; the attributes \(\mathcal{A}\) are the learner state variables; the methods \(\mathcal{M}\) are pedagogical actions; the neural components \(\mathcal{N}\) are SCAM's neural sub-model; the embedding \(\mathcal{E}\) is formalized as three shared-Hilbert-space maps (\(\S\)3.2.2); the identity constraints \(\mathcal{I}\) are the axioms and thresholds; the trigger constraints \(\mathcal{T}\) are formalized as ECA rules, including the safety-gap daemon (\(\S\)3.8); the goal constraints \(\mathcal{G}\) are the constrained objective; and the daemons \(\mathcal{D}\) are formalized as trajectory monitors (\(\S\)5). The ten invisible capabilities are represented as an explicit vector, and ethical competence uses a threshold-gated non-compensatory formulation. Domain competence \(\mathcal{DC}\) is specified as a three-constituent composite of disciplinary mastery, professional performance, and transferable competencies (\(\S\)3.2.3). Flourishing is formalized in two registers: an educational register \(HF_{educational} = f(\mathcal{EC}, \mathcal{ID}, \mathcal{DC})\) and a total register \(HF = HF_{educational} + \epsilon\). Invisible-capacity development is partially compensatory while critical domains are protected by non-regression. Educational success is defined non-monotonically. Relational presence is grounded in Buber, Noddings, and Palmer. SCAM's structured prior and Bayesian update are shown to realize COH's free-energy correspondence when the COH theorem's conjugacy and regularity conditions are met (\(\S\)4.2, Theorem 4.1), and the theory adopts COH's hybrid continuous-discrete formulation (\(\S\)3.9), from which existence and uniqueness follow under the Lipschitz and measurability conditions of Theorem 3.1. A research agenda of four flagship empirical studies is derived, alongside formalizations of the educational safety gap with an interpretation guide. Five limitations are specified. The article positions the framework as a theory of education whose formal structure is portable to broader human-development and AI-governance contexts, while its central claims remain educational.

items.title: A dual-barrier sustained-release hydrogel based on Cu-exchanged Y zeolite and sodium alginate for infected wound healing.
items.authors: Rao Y, Yu X, Xu K, Zheng L, Pu S, Wen N, Wang P, Lin W.
items.abstract: Bacterial wound infection and the growing crisis of antibiotic resistance urgently demand non-antibiotic wound dressings that integrate long-term antibacterial activity and high biosafety. Herein, we designed a dual-barrier sustained-release antibacterial hydrogel (CuY@SA) by embedding Cu2+-exchanged Y zeolite (CuY) into a calcium-crosslinked sodium alginate (SA) matrix. The ordered microporous zeolite acts as the first-stage reservoir to enable intrinsic Cu2+ sustained release via ion exchange, while the alginate network serves as a second physical diffusion barrier to suppress burst release and prolong delivery. The resulting CuY@SA hydrogel eliminated the initial burst and achieved nearly-linear Cu2+ release over 48 h, with an equilibrium swelling ratio of approximately 28 g g-1 in pH 7.4 PBS. In vitro, CuY@SA exhibited over 99.9% bactericidal efficacy against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, while maintaining >98% cytocompatibility with NIH-3T3 fibroblasts at hydrogel concentrations up to 10 mg mL-1. In a mouse full-thickness infected wound model, CuY@SA significantly accelerated wound closure to over 98% by day 14, promoted collagen deposition and re-epithelialization, reduced local inflammation, and caused no obvious organ toxicity or cuproptosis. Compared with the control hydrogel (Cu@SA) containing directly added free Cu2+, CuY@SA showed remarkably lower cytotoxicity and superior in vivo antibacterial activity, confirming the critical role of zeolite in precise controlled release. This work demonstrates that combining an inorganic zeolite carrier with a biopolymer hydrogel provides a simple, scalable, and effective strategy for developing safe and long-acting antibacterial wound dressings. More broadly, it highlights the untapped potential of zeolites as versatile and tunable controlled-release platforms for advanced biomedical applications.

items.title: Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen PET/CT Segmentation Guided by Vision Language Models Embedding Clinical Report Semantics.
items.authors: Pouromidi M, Bayasi N, Samimi R, Hosseinzadeh E, Divband G, Nickkholgh B, Adinehpour Z, Shafiee Dastgerdi S, Rahmim A, Yousefirizi F.
items.abstract: Whole-body prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT segmentation remains challenging: manual contouring is unsustainable, and image-only artificial intelligence models often misclassify physiologic uptake as malignant, causing high false-positive rates. These limitations underscore the need for segmentation strategies that incorporate the nuclear medicine expertise encoded in PET/CT reports but not used by current models. We investigated whether routine PET/CT reports improve automated lesion segmentation for prostate cancer. Methods: We developed a language-guided 3-dimensional SegResNet fusing report text with 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT image features, encoding report semantics via 4 strategies (BiomedVLP, RadGraph, GPT-raw, GPT-engineered) compared with an image-only model (baseline). Of 320 patients who underwent 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, 297 studies were available; 13 were excluded for missing reports or incomplete image-mask pairs, leaving 284 for analysis, split at the patient level into 243 development cases and a fixed 41-case held-out test set. Metrics included Dice, intersection over union (IoU), precision, recall, average symmetric surface distance, 95th percentile Hausdorff distance, surface Dice similarity at 5 mm, and lesion-level false positives, using 3 matching criteria (any overlap; 1-to-1 maximum IoU matching, IoU ≥ 0.5; and correct localization of the SUVmax voxel). Significance was assessed using paired 1-sided Wilcoxon tests with Holm adjustment. Results: Report guidance consistently reduced false positives and improved whole-mask boundary agreement. False-positive lesions were reduced by nearly 4 per patient with BiomedVLP and by approximately 3 per patient with RadGraph and GPT-raw. Average symmetric surface distance decreased from 105.4 ± 62.5 mm (image only) to 23.4 ± 18.2 mm with BiomedVLP, 36.9 ± 22.4 mm with RadGraph, and 36.3 ± 26.4 mm with GPT-raw; 95th percentile Hausdorff distance improved from 455.0 ± 169.3 mm to 123.8 ± 80.3 mm with BiomedVLP, and surface Dice similarity at 5 mm increased from 0.638 ± 0.172 to 0.705 ± 0.181. However, when these surface metrics were recomputed on matched true-positive lesions only using the same 3 criteria, no language-guided model differed significantly from the image-only model for any surface metric (all Holm-adjusted P = 1.0), indicating that the whole-mask improvements were attributable to false-positive suppression rather than genuine gains in contour accuracy on correctly detected lesions. Precision increased for BiomedVLP (0.099) and RadGraph (0.060), with a modest decrease in voxel-level recall (-0.051, BiomedVLP), reflecting a precision-recall trade-off from suppression of spurious uptake. Dice improved by 0.032 but was borderline significant; IoU increased for BiomedVLP (0.036). Lesion-level sensitivity changed by no more than 0.04 for all models and did not reach significance. Total lesion PSMA remained highly correlated with manual measurements (r ≥ 0.85), whereas PSMA tumor volume correlations were more variable across models (r = 0.37-0.70). Conclusion: The integration of PET/CT report semantics into automated PSMA PET/CT segmentation substantially reduced false-positive lesions and preserved total lesion PSMA agreement with manual measurements; a matched true-positive-only reanalysis indicated that the accompanying whole-mask boundary-agreement gains reflected false-positive suppression rather than improved contour accuracy on correctly detected lesions. This approach may reduce manual cleanup and support more reliable quantitative workflows, although precision gains should be weighed against a modest recall reduction. External validation, extension of the true-positive-only analysis to independent cohorts, and PSMA-specific language pretraining are warranted.

items.title: Transformer-based literature-based discovery: Discriminative and generative formulations for Hallmarks of Cancer relationship replication.
items.authors: Cuffy C, Mills L, McInnes BT.
items.abstract:
Objective

Literature-based discovery (LBD) infers implicit relationships that no single document states but that are latent across the literature. Computational LBD has been dominated by methods that embed a biomedical knowledge graph with graph-embedding algorithms. These methods draw on the graph alone, and a concept added to the graph has no representation until the embedding is retrained. We investigate whether contextual transformer encoders address these limitations for closed discovery on the Hallmarks of Cancer (HOC) benchmark.

Methods

We study two formulations of LBD on a shared encoder backbone: a discriminative model that treats discovery as knowledge-graph completion and classifies candidate edges, and a generative model that predicts the embedding of the implicit linking concept and ranks candidates by cosine similarity. We compare both against established baselines, a shallow KGC model (CD-2) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) and similarity-based models, using a ranking protocol and non-parametric significance testing.

Results

Both formulations replicate multiple held-out discoveries and are statistically on par with prior work, while representing any concept that has a text descriptor without retraining, which the graph-embedding baselines cannot do. A general-domain encoder (BERT) is competitive with, and on one dataset exceeds, its domain-adapted counterpart (BioBERT), and input scaling helps the generative but harms the discriminative formulation.

Conclusion

Contextual encoders are viable for LBD, and how the task is posed shapes discovery-replication performance.

items.title: Mapping five decades of the evolution and digital transformation of WASH tools for low-income and fragile contexts.
items.authors: Elkhider M, Domini M, Vaccari M.
items.abstract: This review synthesises more than five decades of Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) tool evolution, from the analogue, hardware-centred instruments of the 1970s to contemporary digital platforms and early AI-enabled applications through 2025. Drawing on a semi-systematic search of academic, institutional, and grey literature, the paper maps major tools, their functions and digital maturity, across water supply, sanitation, hygiene, and solid waste management, with a focus on low-income and fragile contexts. Analysis reveals a progression from paper-based checklists and technical guides in the 1970s to structured monitoring and participatory planning instruments in the 1990s-2000s, followed by mobile-enabled and digital systems in recent years. Findings show that water-supply tools are comparatively mature and digitally advanced, sanitation tools remain the least digitally integrated and underrepresented, and solid waste management exhibits high functional diversity but uneven digital uptake. Since 2010, integrated instruments have emerged that link WASH with climate risk and public health; a small number of tools now incorporate predictive analytics and remote sensing, but AI and IoT applications remain nascent in resource-constrained and fragile contexts. The review identifies gaps in empirical evaluation, digital readiness, scalability, and governance alignment, and highlights factors that influence tool uptake-such as institutional embedding and donor support. The review informs developers and organizations on future innovation and global application of tools to accelerate equitable, scalable digital transformation of WASH services in low-income and humanitarian settings.

items.title: Latent Representation Learning from 3D Brain MRI for Latent Analysis and Prediction in Multiple Sclerosis.
items.authors: Ngoc Huynh T, Duc Kien N, Thai Ninh D, Hai Anh N, Hiep Dinh T, Vaneckova M, Uher T, Schependom JV, Denissen S, Quoc Long T, Linh Trung N, Nagels G.
items.abstract:
Background

Neurological diseases can lead to significant cognitive impairment. Linking magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived measures of brain structure with clinical assessments of cognitive function remains challenging, as conventional statistical methods and traditional machine learning approaches may struggle to capture complex relationships between brain structure and cognitive outcomes, hindering the development of reliable imaging biomarkers. Although deep learning methods offer greater predictive capabilities, their black-box nature limits interpretability, posing a major obstacle to clinical translation.

New method

Latent representation learning via generative models can provide informative representations and support deeper analysis and cognitive biomarker prediction. While standard generative adversarial networks and diffusion models primarily focus on generating images from random noise, variational autoencoders offer compact, probabilistic latent representations that are well suited for downstream tasks. In this study, we propose InfoVAE-Med3D, an adaptation of the InfoVAE framework for three-dimensional brain ​MRI to learn informative latent representations. By explicitly relaxing the mutual information regularization penalty between inputs and latent representations, our method aims to capture richer information from input MRI data, facilitating the analysis of brain-related characteristics and downstream prediction.

Results

We evaluate InfoVAE-Med3D on two datasets: a healthy control dataset ([Formula: see text]) containing chronological age and sex information, and a Multiple Sclerosis (MS) dataset ([Formula: see text]) collected from the Multiple Sclerosis Center of the First Medical Faculty, Charles University, Prague, containing chronological age, sex, and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) scores. The learned latent representations capture information related to sex and brain volumetric features, including grey and white matter volumes, as reflected in sex-related clustering and smooth transitions in brain volume measures in two-dimensional visualizations. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that InfoVAE-Med3D learns more informative latent representations, especially when the mutual information regularization penalty is completely removed. In this setting, the model generally outperforms other variational autoencoder variants in both MRI reconstruction and prediction of brain age and SDMT scores using support vector regression, while remaining competitive with deep learning-based predictive models, particularly on the MS dataset.

Conclusion

InfoVAE-Med3D provides informative latent representations from brain MRI data of both healthy controls and patients with MS. By improving predictive performance and providing interpretable insights into the learned latent representations, the proposed framework offers a promising approach for advancing biomarker discovery and the analysis of cognitive impairment in neurological diseases, particularly ​MS.

items.title: Embedding the Cultural Health Navigator Model: A Health System-Integrated Approach for Refugee Care.
items.authors: Azugbene EA, Nizigiyimana JF, Schuster RC, Coonrod DV, Johnson-Agbakwu CE.
items.abstract: Resettled refugees and culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) populations face persistent barriers to health care, including linguistic constraints, cultural disconnects, and limited availability of system-integrated approaches responsive to their needs. This article presents the Cultural Health Navigator (CHN) model, a health system-integrated community health worker (CHW) approach developed within an Arizona Medicaid-integrated public safety-net hospital system. The model embeds trained, multilingual CHNs within clinical workflows to provide culturally and linguistically responsive navigation, health education, care coordination, medical interpretation, and linkage to clinical and community resources. We apply the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) retrospectively to describe the model's implementation features and use the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) framework to guide prospective evaluation. The CHN model integrates CHW certification, clinical workflows, community partnerships, electronic health record infrastructure, and Medicaid reimbursement pathways to support implementation and sustainability. Preliminary evidence from the program supports continued evaluation of its potential contributions to patient navigation, trust, health literacy, health care utilization, and maternal and newborn health. We present the CHN model as a practice-based, potentially transferable implementation approach that health systems can adapt to strengthen culturally responsive care for refugees and other CALD populations. Future evaluation should establish its effectiveness, sustainability, and transferability across diverse health care settings.

items.title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
items.authors: Heredia EA, Papasian L, Paine J, Patre S, Jonsson TJ, Keller T, Fang Z, Narumi VH, Katiyar I, Lagerstrom IT, Lombardo J, Simental B, Tran B, Sibrian D, Castellanos O, Wells J, Lee JSH, Shriver C, Agus DB, Basho R, Matasci N.
items.abstract: Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI (≥30 kg/m  2 ) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m  2 ) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73-0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor-stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

items.title: Does Graph Structure Improve AI-Generated Text Detection? A Controlled Audit with Tuned Baselines
items.authors: Alaktif A, Chergui M, Faiq G, Ammoumou A.
items.abstract: Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

items.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES.
items.authors: Pourmirzaei M, Alqarghuli S, Chen K, Pourmirzaei M, Xu D.
items.abstract:
Motivation

Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training.

Results

Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

Availability and implementation

The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand. The datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604.

Supplementary information

Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

items.title: CuCo-N-C nanozyme-mediated hydrogel colorimetric platform: dual-reading modes of ratiometry and smartphone for nitrite detection.
items.authors: Wang G, Song C, Ma S, Lu C, Sun J, He Y.
items.abstract: As a potentially hazardous food additive, nitrite acts as a double-edged sword, since excessive intake can trigger severe health risks. Developing an efficient and convenient on-site detection method for nitrite in food is therefore of great significance, yet remains challenging. To address this issue, a dual-mode colorimetric platform integrating a ratiometric assay with a hydrogel-based sensor has been constructed on the basis of the high oxidase-like activity of CuCo-N-C nanozymes. These nanozymes catalyze dissolved oxygen to oxidize colorless 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) into blue ox-TMB. The addition of nitrite triggers a diazotization reaction with ox-TMB, leading to decreased absorbance at 652 nm and increased absorbance at 450 nm. Furthermore, a smartphone-assisted portable kit was fabricated by embedding CuCo-N-C and TMB within an agarose hydrogel, enabling on-site visual quantification of nitrite in traditional foods including ham sausage, preserved eggs, salted duck eggs, mustard and fermented bean curd. This dual-mode colorimetric system is simple and reliable, with portable hardware and easy operation, and holds promise as a sensing platform for food safety monitoring.

items.title: CAB-LA PrEP Prescriptions and Abandonment in the United States, January 2022-June 2025.
items.authors: Zhu W, Patel RR, Huang YA, Davis NL, Hoover KW, Kourtis AP.
items.abstract:
Background

Injectable long-acting cabotegravir (CAB-LA) for HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2021. A national assessment of CAB-LA PrEP abandonment, defined as not filling any prescription, could inform national PrEP implementation efforts.

Methods

We conducted a national observational cohort study using IQVIA Longitudinal Prescription data to characterize persons prescribed CAB-LA or daily oral PrEP (DO-PrEP) in the United States during January 2022-June 2025. We compared 6-month abandonment risk among individuals with an index CAB-LA or DO-PrEP prescription during 2022-2024. Associations were estimated using multivariable modified Poisson regression models and reported as adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

The number of individuals prescribed CAB-LA PrEP increased from 4,645 in 2022 to 23,378 in 2024 and 25,018 during January-June 2025. The proportion of individuals receiving CAB-LA increased from 0.1% in quarter 1 of 2022 to 5.4% in quarter 2 of 2025. While women had a higher 6-month PrEP abandonment risk than men, regardless of PrEP regimen, they were less likely to abandon CAB-LA (11.9%) than DO-PrEP (18.1%, aRR=0.68, 95% CI: 0.62-0.74). The opposite was observed for men, with men more likely to abandon CAB-LA PrEP (10.2%) than DO-PrEP (8.1%, aRR=1.25, 95% CI: 1.20-1.31).

Conclusions

CAB-LA PrEP prescribing increased steadily during the first 3.5 years after approval; abandonment risk differed by PrEP regimen and sex. Addressing barriers to injectable and daily oral PrEP uptake, and strengthening sex-specific PrEP implementation strategies, may further reduce abandonment risk.

items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Cabotegravir Long-Acting HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): A Systematic Review of Modelling Studies.
items.authors: Effiong FB, Olawuyi DA, Effiong BB, Adeyemi AV, Ekpor E, Dine RD, Inaku KO.
items.abstract:
Objectives

Cabotegravir long-acting injectable (CAB-LA) is a promising non-oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention, especially where daily oral adherence is poor. Despite superior efficacy, CAB-LA's high price raises concerns about economic value and implementation across settings. This study reviewed modelling studies on CAB-LA's cost-effectiveness as PrEP across diverse populations and settings.

Methods

We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase and Cochrane Library (2015-2025), assessing CAB-LA's cost-effectiveness versus oral PrEP or no PrEP. Eligible studies reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, cost per HIV infection averted, or cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) or disability-adjusted life year gained. Reporting quality was assessed using the CHEERS 2022 checklist. Results were narratively synthesized due to heterogeneity.

Results

Eleven modelling studies across sub-Saharan Africa, the United States, and Asia-Pacific showed that CAB-LA averted more HIV infections than oral PrEP, especially in high-incidence, low-adherence populations. In high-risk U.S. populations, CAB-LA averted about 71,000 infections and gained 4.65 million QALYs. In Africa, CAB-LA became economically favourable under lower acquisition-cost assumptions, although cost-effective prices varied across models, populations, price years and thresholds. U.S. and Asia-Pacific models found CAB-LA not cost-effective at current prices, requiring 24-88% price reductions. Sensitivity and scenario analyses showed that cost-effectiveness estimates were responsive to CAB-LA price, HIV incidence, ART coverage, adherence, persistence, and programme-delivery assumptions.

Conclusion

CAB-LA cost-effectiveness is context dependent and generally more favourable at lower prices, higher-incidence populations, and poor oral PrEP adherence. Wider adoption may require strategies to improve economic value, equitable access, and implementation, especially in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Real-World Durability of Long-Acting Cabotegravir PrEP in Choice-Driven and Indication-Driven Users.
items.authors: Moschese D, Esvan R, Fusetti C, Micheli G, Lazzarin S, Farinacci D, Giacomelli A, Barchi V, Cossu MV, Giacinta A, Oreni L, Caruso F, Antinori A, Gori A, Mazzotta V.
items.abstract:
Objectives

To evaluate real-world adherence, persistence, and discontinuation of CAB-LA PrEP among individuals accessing this strategy either by choice or due to clinical or behavioural indications associated with challenges to oral PrEP.

Methods

We conducted an observational cohort study including 388 individuals initiating CAB-LA PrEP between December 2024 and November 2025 at two Italian referral centres. Adherence to the injection schedule, persistence over time, and all-cause and drug-related discontinuations were assessed overall and stratified by access modality.

Results

Adherence exceeded 94.9% across almost all assessed injection time points. Overall persistence remained high, with 87.9% (95% CI 84.7-91.2%) of participants remaining on CAB-LA PrEP at week 52 [84.1% (95% CI 77.0-91.3%) in choice- and 89.3% (95% CI 85.7-92.9%) in indication-driven users; p=0.191]. All-cause discontinuation occurred in 12.1% of participants, while drug-related discontinuations were uncommon (6.9%).

Conclusions

CAB-LA PrEP demonstrated high adherence, sustained persistence, and low rates of drug-related discontinuation in routine clinical practice. Durable performance regardless of access modality supports its feasibility both as a preference-sensitive option and as an alternative for populations experiencing difficulties with oral prevention.

items.title: Equitable expansion of PrEP Choice for transgender women and travestis in Brazil: Community and other stakeholder perspectives on implementation opportunities
items.authors: Zamudio-Haas SA, Saggese GSR, Barros D, Cezaretto A, Prado PV, Rodriguez J, Menezes NP, Veras MA, Lippman SA.
items.abstract: Expanding prevention programs to incorporate new PrEP modalities could offer important benefits to transgender women and travestis (TWT) in Brazil, who are underserved by current approaches. Long-acting injectable (LAI) products are not yet available through the national health system, and episodic PrEP was recently approved for some TWT, providing a critical window for formative research to guide equitable rollout. Engaging the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, we interviewed TWT PrEP consumers (8), PrEP providers (8), and program/policy advisors (4) in São Paulo. Participants expressed enthusiasm for offering all modalities as a cohesive ‘PrEP choice’ intervention– despite consensus on advantages of LAI-products (increased ease, freedom, protection) and limitations of episodic PrEP (complicated dosing, limited eligibility). We differentiated implementation opportunities related to culture, learning climate, and readiness in neighborhood primary care clinics, referral centers, and community-based programs. Findings coalesced around the need to center community in planning and executing implementation processes, by incorporating adjunctive interventions (pain management, peer navigation, food and transportation assistance) and peer staff. By interviewing stakeholders who participated in LAI-PrEP research, we elicited informed perspectives grounded in lived experience, before widespread availability. Findings provide a foundation for future studies comparing implementation and outcomes for TWT in different delivery settings.

items.title: The missing link in the blue economy: Empowering the next generation through blue skills and ocean literacy
items.authors: Canning-Clode J, Esson D, Monteiro J, Dinis A, Andrade C, Alves F, Gueroun S, Vieira D, Nunes P, Mossae B, Tuda A, Napper I, Wilson A, Tudhope A.

items.title: CGHA-Net: Context-guided hybrid attention for hierarchical representation learning in medical image segmentation.
items.authors: Yang X, Hou J, Deng L, Huang S.
items.abstract: Medical image segmentation aims to precisely identify and separate anatomical components and lesion regions in medical scans, and it constitutes a core technique for clinical diagnosis, disease evaluation, and organ morphological analysis. However, accurate segmentation of complex anatomical regions remains a significant challenge because of considerable differences in object scale, indistinct boundaries, and insufficient tissue contrast in medical images. These issues often limit the ability of existing methods to effectively exploit global semantic representations while simultaneously retaining detailed local information. Reliable segmentation of organs and lesions remains challenging in practical medical images because low contrast, irregular morphology, and blurred boundaries can obscure target structures and hinder accurate delineation. To address these challenges, we propose a new medical image segmentation framework, termed CGHA-Net. First, a context-guided semantic enhancement module is incorporated into the skip connections, in which deep global semantic information is progressively used to enhance shallow feature representations, thereby improving semantic discriminability while preserving local details. Second, a multidimensional semantic fusion module is introduced in the decoder to enhance contextual feature representations by jointly integrating spatial, channel, and orientation-aware information, thereby enhancing boundary detail reconstruction. Finally, a largest connected component loss is proposed to encourage the continuity and integrity of the segmented regions. Across several public benchmarks for medical image segmentation, overall, CGHA-Net achieves competitive results among leading approaches, suggesting satisfactory effectiveness and generalization capability.

items.title: How Solvent Approximations Affect the Learnability of Molecular Polarizability and Hyperpolarizability Tensors: A Study on Embedded Water Clusters.
items.authors: Ramos TN, Champagne B.
items.abstract: Machine-learning (ML) models have shown considerable success in predicting molecular properties from atomic structures. Yet, it remains unclear how to represent solvent-induced effects when targeting optical response properties strongly influenced by the environment. Here, we investigate how different solvent approximations affect the learnability of molecular polarizability (α) and first hyperpolarizability (β) tensors in embedded water clusters. Using a multiscale framework inspired by sequential quantum chemistry/molecular mechanics partitioning, the quantum chemistry (QC) and molecular mechanics (MM) regions are encoded separately through symmetry-adapted λ-SOAP descriptors and combined within kernel ridge regression models. The same descriptor family is employed on the same structures for all solvent representations, allowing the influence of the solvent approximation on model learnability to be isolated. Three embedding schemes are considered: electrostatic embedding (EE), polarizable embedding (PE), and polarizable embedding including effective external field corrections (PE-EEF). ML models that separately encode QC and MM regions outperform single-descriptor representations, indicating that the relevant structural information is distributed across multiple spatial scales. Increasing the sophistication of the solvent approximation generally reduces predictive accuracy, despite identical molecular structures, suggesting that polarization effects are only partially recoverable from structural descriptors alone. Analysis of optimized descriptor hyperparameters further reveals a shift toward larger spatial ranges and richer angular resolutions as solvent polarization effects are introduced. Although microscopic tensor predictions become more challenging for PE and PE-EEF, ensemble distributions of experimentally relevant observables derived from the α and β tensors remain well reproduced. These results provide insight into the relationship between solvent representations and ML learnability and highlight the importance of multiscale representations for modeling solvent-dependent optical response properties.

items.title: Interpretable Graph Neural Networks for Structure-activity-based Prediction of Drug-induced Toxicity and Adverse Reactions.
items.authors: Sanaye P, Sanaye M, Devadkar K.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Drug-induced toxicity and Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) remain major barriers to safe pharmacotherapy and often arise unpredictably. Existing ADR prediction models primarily rely on population-scale data, limiting early detection and mechanistic interpretability.

Methods

We investigated whether molecular graph topology combined with attention mechanisms could explain variance in SIDER ADR labels. Drugs were represented as molecular graphs derived from SMILES, enriched with atomic-level physicochemical descriptors and Morgan fingerprints. An attention mechanism quantified the relative contribution of graph substructures and global molecular features. The proposed model, AttentionADR, was trained and evaluated solely on curated ADR labels without using clinical text or omics data.

Results

AttentionADR achieved robust performance (micro ROC-AUC = 0.82; weighted recall = 0.78). Graph-based structural representations consistently received the highest attention weights, whereas physicochemical descriptors and fingerprints contributed minimally. Performance was highest for skin (F1 = 0.9464) and nervous system disorders (F1 = 0.9386), while respiratory disorders showed comparatively lower performance (AUC = 0.69), reflecting structural diversity across System Organ Classes.

Discussion

These findings highlight the central role of molecular topology in capturing patterns associated with drug-induced adverse effects and demonstrate the value of attention-based models for interpretable, structure-informed drug safety assessment. Because structural signals vary across ADR classes, predictions should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive.

Conclusion

From a translational standpoint, because AttentionADR requires only a candidate molecule's structure, it offers medicinal chemists and pharmaceutical safety teams a low-cost, interpretable triage tool that can flag likely ADR liabilities during early-stage lead optimization, before experimental toxicology or population-scale clinical data are available, thereby supporting faster and better informed acceptance decisions in drug discovery.

items.title: AI Governance in Health Information Practice: A Practical Framework for HIPAA-Compliant AI Adoption.
items.authors: Stokes TM, Houser SH.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being integrated into health information workflows, including clinical documentation, coding support, revenue cycle operations, and patient engagement systems. While these technologies offer efficiency and enhanced decision support, their use introduces new privacy, security, and compliance risks when protected health information is entered as input, processed by third-party systems, or incorporated into AI-generated outputs. Existing Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliance structures do not address the complexities of AI-enabled environments, creating governance gaps that expose health care organizations to regulatory and operational risk. This article presents a practical governance framework that integrates AI oversight into existing HIPAA compliance programs. Drawing on compliance literature, regulatory guidance, and emerging AI governance models, the framework adapts core elements of the Office of Inspector General compliance model to address AI-specific risks. We proposed AI-centered policies and procedures, governance leadership, workforce training, auditing and monitoring, and incident response planning. This article provides implementation guidance tailored to health information practice, including workflow-based examples and phased adoption strategies. By positioning AI governance as an extension of established information governance responsibilities, health information professionals can proactively safeguard patient privacy, strengthen regulatory compliance, and support responsible innovation in AI-enabled health care environments.

items.title: Metabolic signature combined with changes in proteome and transcriptome shape respiratory syncytial virus infection and response to vaccination in a bovine model.
items.authors: Kothadiya S, Mathew AP, Schoofs AD, Nandu RK, Niolo-Velesaca CA, McGill J, Bardhan R.
items.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major respiratory disease in infants leading to long-term morbidity. Bovine RSV (bRSV) serves as a clinically translatable large animal model to understand host responses in neonates to vaccination and re-infection enabling straightforward and accessible sample collection not often possible in human infants. This study probes clinically relevant bovine biointerfaces by combining Raman spectroscopy-based metabolic profiling with proteomics and gene expression in nasal fluid, serum, and lung tissues collected from 11 vaccinated (V) and 11 non-vaccinated (NV) neonatal calves following bRSV rechallenge. The analyses showed at Day 7 post-challenge, 16 significant Raman metabolite peaks in nasal fluid, 17 peaks in sera, and 17 peaks in lesioned lung tissue differentiated V from NV calves including features associated with glucose, lipids and fatty acids, and phenylalanine among others. We find that in NV calves systemic metabolic changes were greater than in the V group, and in an exploratory proteomic analysis of a subset of animals (n = 4/group), we identified a complement and innate immune protein signature in NV calves that aligned with metabolic features. In lesioned lung tissue, immune engagement between V and NV calves differed with changes observed in multiple metabolites that tightly correlated with gene expression and showed higher inflammatory cytokine gene expression (IL17A, IL6, IFNγ, IFNβ, IL8) in NV calves. Collectively, our data show an integrative approach enables a comprehensive molecular view of translationally relevant biointerfaces to understand vaccination and reinfection-associated host response. The outcomes of this study can be leveraged in the long-term to understand treatment response in human RSV.

items.title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
items.authors: Srinivasan B, Nazar S, Gandhi V, Zhang E, Bachvaroff T, Kolmogorov M, Place A, Firtina C.
items.abstract:
Summary:

Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91—0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Placental Pathology: From Spatial Analytics to Molecular Proxies
items.authors: Adu-Gyamfi EA, Twumasi A.
items.abstract: The placenta is a crucial determinant of the success of pregnancy. However, manual evaluation of its pathology is limited by poor reproducibility and a global shortage of specialized perinatal pathologists. Besides, predicting recurrent pregnancy complications remains highly challenging, which severely limits the timely deployment of proactive therapeutic interventions. Automated artificial intelligence screening of the delivered placenta will help to overcome these bottlenecks. In this work, we synthesize the transition toward self-supervised Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) that yield robust, stain-agnostic tissue embeddings. Furthermore, we evaluate the emergence of Non-Euclidean Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that map cellular topologies to quantify mal-perfusion, alongside multimodal generative cross-attention networks (MGCN) that integrate gigapixel histology with electronic medical records (EMR) to improve pregnancy risk stratification. Moreover, we propose a novel, functional systems-biology framework to retroactively bridge digital morphometrics – such as impaired trophoblast fusion and invasion – to upstream dysregulated molecular cascades, including the ERK1/2–DUSP, FAK–MAPK, and HIF-1α regulatory axes. Finally, we address translational bottlenecks – such as diagnostic inter-observer variation, systemic clinical confounders, and geographic data bias – and outline hardware edge-deployment strategies for the pathology floor. Ultimately, automated placental screening will help to reveal immediate newborn developmental risks and maternal pathological recurrence risks across subsequent pregnancies. Together, these computational paradigms offer a potential translational roadmap to standardize digital placental pathology into a personalized reproductive medicine pillar.

items.title: Evidence-based policy improvements for lipid lowering therapy: a focus on reducing clinical inertia and improving cardiovascular outcomes.
items.authors: Chen RT, Lan NSR, Watts GF, Ray KK, Pagidipati NJ, Bhatt AS, Nicholls SJ, Nelson AJ.
items.abstract:
Introduction

Despite substantial evidence linking low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) reduction to improved cardiovascular outcomes, a significant implementation gap persists. Clinical inertia, defined as failure to initiate or intensify therapy despite suboptimal control, remains a key barrier to achieving guideline-recommended LDL-C goals, particularly in high-risk populations.

Areas covered

This review analyses systemic drivers of clinical inertia in lipid management, with emphasis on modifiable policy and organizational barriers. These include restrictive access and reimbursement policies, suboptimal health information technology and workflow design, misaligned quality metrics, and fragmented care delivery models. Evidence-based strategies to address these barriers are evaluated, including administrative reform, financial incentives, integrated clinical decision support, team-based care, and structured care pathways.

Expert opinion

The principal challenge is not therapeutic efficacy but effective implementation. Translating evidence into population benefit requires a shift from isolated prescribing to system-level optimization. Key priorities include harmonizing access policies with guidelines, embedding outcome-based accountability, and scaling multidisciplinary care models. Sustained adherence also depends on addressing patient-level beliefs, treatment tolerability and burden, and broader socio-economic barriers, including social determinants of health. Over the next five years, progress will depend on integrating implementation science, digital tools, and value-based frameworks to enable proactive, equitable, and sustainable lipid control.

items.title: Model cards are not primary artifacts: stereochemistry in the MoLFormer and SMI-TED chemical foundation models.
items.authors: Kaplan N.
items.abstract: Pretrained chemical language models are selected, embedded with, and fine tuned on the basis of what their documentation says they are. We report that the released model card for MoLFormer, one of the most widely used chemical foundation models, states that isomeric information was removed from its training data, and that this statement is contradicted by artifacts distributed in the model's own repository. The shipped token frequency table records the tetrahedral stereocentre token [C@H] occurring 669,642,207 times, making it the twelfth most frequent token in a corpus of 47.2 billion tokens, ahead of fluorine, and stereochemical tokens account for 3.17% of all token occurrences. The described stripping is real but occurs at a different pipeline stage: isomeric = False is hardcoded into the fine tuning scripts and applied to downstream benchmark data, not to pretraining. We find a related divergence in SMI-TED, whose released vocabulary contains 2,393 tokens rather than the 2,988 reported, and whose shipped frequency table is identical to MoLFormer's, byte for byte, across all 2,357 shared tokens, despite the paper describing a different corpus. We release the extracted frequency table and an audit tool, and recommend that chemical model cards state stereochemistry handling separately for pretraining, fine tuning, and inference.

items.title: Foundation-model imaging biomarkers for pancreatic cancer: cross-species discovery of conserved tumour biology in mouse MRI and human CT.
items.authors: Yu G, Zhang Z, Eresen A, Hou Q, Wei P, Hou X, Tian L, Webster S, Liu R, Nauli SM, Yu J, Yaghmai V, Zhang Z.
items.abstract:
Background

Computed tomography (CT) stages pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) but does not read out the treatment-guiding tumour biology, requiring biopsy. Whether an imaging-biology relationship discovered in preclinical MRI holds independently in human CT is unknown.

Methods

One pipeline was applied to two PDAC cohorts: longitudinal 9.4 T multi-parametric MRI (169 sessions; 1002 image series, 471 quantitative maps) with terminal histopathology in male C57BL/6 mice bearing orthotopic KPC-derived tumours treated with gemcitabine, a dendritic-cell vaccine, both, or neither, and abdominal CT with matched proteogenomics from CPTAC-PDA. Radiomics and frozen foundation-model embeddings were modelled under grouped cross-validation against five pre-specified paired endpoints, with no cross-species transfer of features, weights, or labels.

Findings

Applied independently, the pipeline recovered four matched molecular endpoints in both species (CD8 infiltration, stromal collagen, CD8:CD68 immune balance, cytolytic activity), with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.938-0.960 in mice and 0.780-0.856 in humans. Survival concordance indices were 0.729 and 0.689. After adjustment for age, stage, and grade, the human imaging score remained independently prognostic (hazard ratio 1.87 per SD, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.66; p < 0.001 [Wald test]; combined concordance index 0.726 versus 0.611 for clinical covariates). Findings held in portal-venous-restricted analysis; frozen embeddings outperformed end-to-end fine-tuning in both arms.

Interpretation

One pipeline recovered matched PDAC biology in mouse MRI and human CT, supporting preclinical imaging to nominate non-invasive CT biomarker candidates for biopsy-sparing PDAC trial stratification, pending prospective external validation.

Funding

National Cancer Institute; Society of Interventional Radiology Foundation; University of California Irvine Anticancer Challenge Pilot grant.

items.title: Robotic Rollator Assistance for Sit-to-Stand Transfers in Older Adults with Mobility Challenges: Within-Participant Feasibility Study.
items.authors: Mahdi A, Buchner T, Werner C, Hu Y, Mombaur K.
items.abstract:
Background

Robotic mobility aids with sit-to-stand (STS) support may help older adults reduce physical effort during a demanding, fall-prone daily task.

Objective

This paper reports a feasibility evaluation of the "SkyWalker" robotic walker, which provides powered STS assistance via actuated lower handles. The 2 trajectories (linear and S-shape) were selected to examine how assistance profile shape influences feasibility, biomechanics, and user experience.

Methods

Seven older adult patients with mobility challenges were enrolled from a rehabilitation hospital. One withdrew during the robot familiarization (unable to stand up) without attempting any study trial, and 6 completers (4 women, 2 men; aged 70-84 years) form the analyzed sample. Participants completed 3 within-subject conditions: SkyWalker with the linear trajectory, SkyWalker with the S-shape trajectory, and a conventional rollator. We quantified STS task performance, perceived exertion Borg Category-Ratio 10 scale (Borg CR10), kinematics (center-of-gravity [CoG] height), kinetics (vertical ground-reaction force [Fz], normalized to body weight), and technology acceptance using an adapted Tele-healthcare Satisfaction Questionnaire-Wearable Technology (TSQ-WT). Participant-level data are the primary presentation. Condition effects were tested with exact nonparametric tests.

Results

Under linear assistance, 27 of 30 repetitions (90%) were successful (mean 4.50, SD 0.84; 4 of 6 participants at 5/5) and perceived exertion was the lowest of the 3 conditions (Borg CR10 mean 1.50, SD 1.38; lower than the rollator in 3 of 6 participants, unchanged in 2, higher in 1). Under S-shape assistance, 21 of 30 repetitions (70%) were successful (mean 3.50, SD 1.97; 3 of 6 at 5/5), with exertion comparable to the conventional rollator (mean 2.50, SD 2.43 vs mean 2.33, SD 1.63). All 6 completers achieved 5 of 5 repetitions with the conventional rollator, so robotic assistance did not increase the number of successful transfers in this cohort. Exact tests showed no significant condition effect on exertion (Friedman χ22=2.1; exact P=.40; Kendall W=0.18) or success (Friedman χ22=5.0, exact P=.11; Kendall W=0.42). Group CoG curves showed earlier, more monotonic elevation for linear, and per-participant Fz showed greater between-participant variability in load-transfer timing under S-shape. Technology acceptance was heterogeneous (TSQ-WT totals 22-77 of 80; 4 of 6 participants at 64 or higher).

Conclusions

Powered STS assistance was feasible for most assisted transfers: 27 of 30 repetitions (90%) succeeded under the linear trajectory, which also produced the lowest mean perceived effort of the 3 conditions. The S-shape trajectory was more demanding, producing more partial completions and no effort reduction relative to the conventional rollator. In this first evaluation of SkyWalker with its intended users, the assistance profile, not powered assistance itself, is the variable to prioritize in further testing, and the results, which motivate trajectory personalization and brief familiarization, are informing the design of the next SkyWalker generation.

items.title: Horizon-Aware Forecasting of Hypertension Prevalence and Mean Total Cholesterol in Chinese Men: Retrospective Leakage-Controlled Benchmark Study Comparing Statistical, Machine-Learning, and Neural Models.
items.authors: Lai W, Subhan F, Zhou N, Khan J.
items.abstract:
Background

Forecasts of population-level cardiovascular risk factors can support surveillance and planning, but annual country-level health series are often short. With only 30 or 39 annual values per target, model flexibility can outpace the information available for training, making leakage control, repeated temporal evaluation, and comparison with simple baselines essential.

Objective

The aim of this study is to compare statistical, classical machine-learning, and neural forecasting models for age-standardized prevalence of hypertension (ASPH) and mean total cholesterol (MTC) in Chinese men and to test whether attention or substantially greater neural capacity provides consistent predictive benefit.

Methods

The authors analyzed 2 officially sourced annual series: ASPH for Chinese men aged 30 to 79 years (1990-2019; 30 observations) and MTC for Chinese men aged 18 years or older (1980-2018; 39 observations). No series was interpolated, extrapolated, imputed, smoothed, spliced, or synthetically extended. Leakage-controlled expanding-window evaluation began after 21 observations and assessed 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons. Classical machine-learning and neural models used a fixed primary lookback of 3 (L=3), with nested lookback selection disabled; neural models used 10 fixed seeds. Performance was assessed with root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error, mean absolute scaled error, root mean squared scaled error, symmetric mean absolute percentage error, directional accuracy, mean error, median error, diagnostic R², prespecified neural-ablation inference, empirical forecast-interval coverage, and computational-cost reporting.

Results

Statistical models had the lowest RMSE in all 6 target-horizon cells.
